CHAPTER I. It was the middle of the afternoon, still, calm, breathless with heat, and in the centre of a green expanse' of sea ship was slowly sinking. Upon the deck, apart from the groups of haggard people making for the boats, stood a man and a girl. The girl was beautiful—more than beautiful; and to the man, middle-aged though he was, hard, and cold, and stern, with grey in his hair and straight lines about his mouth, there was something in her face that set his heart beating as he looked at her—some- thing that stirred his pulse against his will, for he hated women. "Are you sure there is no hope?" She had laid a white hand on his arm, and looked with desperate eyes into his. "Are you sure we 'can't be saved?" she asked, breathlessly. He looked down into her face and then away. Before them, blue, smooth, and still, lay the epen sea. Above them the sky smiled' „down cruelly at the White 'faces upon that sinking vessel, and below them waited certain death. Another hour—less—might see them adrift upon the open water. Another day the ship upon which they stood would be under the waves. Already John Deere fancied he could feel the thrill of timbers underfoot. Already he seemed to see the shiver that would run over the great boat when she gave her final leap civ,;rn to the deep waters. For a moment he made no answer. Then ho pointed to the boats swinging out, ready to be lowered. A loosening of the ropes—a minute's work—would launch them, and the small crowds ef people stood nervously before each, waiting for the captain's order. But he was hoping against hope that help would come. High up on his bridge he swept the ocean for a glimpse of some passing vessel. Haggard eyes followed the sweep of the tele- scope and saw nothing but the empty, pitiless sea and sky. It was a_ most beautiful day—this day of death, hot, and still, and smiling. "No, there is no hope," said Dr. John Deere, suddenly, at last. "The boat is doomed." - "Yes, but—l can't believe it," cried the.girl. Her voice broke huskily, and the doctor looked down a little curiously into her beauti- ful face. She Puzzled him. She was too beautiful to be travelling alone—too wonderfully beautiful for the peace of men's Minds as he had seen even in those four short weeks since they had left Australia. , She had boarded the boat alone—perhaps new she was going to her death alone= and from the time she took her first meal 41 the dining- room almost every man 'on board had been ready to throw himself 'at her feet. • Yet that there was some strange mystery behind her—something strange in her life—some- thing queer behind the magic beauty of her dark eyes, John Dacr'e felt convinced, and as he looked at her a certain coldness crept into his glance. . "We can none of us believe he said. "Nevertheless, to-night we shall he out in small boats on the open sea, at the mercy of the winds and the waves, unles's we hail a passing ship very soon now." "But—but—surely they can find out where the damage is, and mend it in time?" she ,asked,

John Dacre shook his head. "Every effort has been mad d and has failed," he said. "The boat is doomed, and, Miss Murray, it is Well that we make up our minds to face what may be death with steady minds and brave hearts. We are out of our course, and the chance of sight- ing a vess\el is small. We may drift about for days in the open boats, or we -may—" He broke off. The girl shivered suddenly, and did not turn when lie pointed. "Look, Miss Murray, the women and children -will he put in the boats directly. You should go forward now—" " I can't !'• she startled him suddenly. Her hand, white and shaking, grasped his coat with a clutch that bewildered him, it was so fierce, - so savage. "I can't!" Her voice was broken and husky.." I—l—may never reach- land. I I believe—oh ! I may die, apd I must speak—l must speak before I go. I thust speak.to you!" -He looked down curiously. -Again that strange feeling ran over him, that behind her lay some hidden mystery—something perhaps appalling. Her hand still clung to his arm. B.e put his own upon it. "Miss Murray, if I can help you "he began ;_ .but she dragged. her hand suddenly away, and, going Over to the side of the boat, clung to the rail, staring with suddenly haggard eyes over the empty sea, staring into the sun- thiffe, seeing what horrors he did not know. He followed her slowly. Further along the deck above them a sudden movement had taken place among the passengers. The women were being put' into the boats. "Miss Murray!" he cried. She turned abruptly. "I must 33.3 quick," she gasped, breathlessly. "There—there are only a few minutes now, -I suppose, but there is one thing I want you to promise first—" - "Yes 7" he asked, with his eyes fixed curi- ously on her beautiful face. "Yes, Miss Murray ? " "I want you to 'promise—to try to keep what I am going to tell you from Sir Geoffrey Verri- ker." She lifted her eyes suddenly, with a faint flush creeping over her cheeks as she met his cold, hard glance. " ! promise me you will do that? You will never understand me; perhaps even you will hate to think that I have ever touched you, but, oh! I have had no chance—l. have never .had a chance!" She flung out her Arms. "Unfortunate from tile beginning, I am unfor- tunate to the end—except for one thing." Her face lighted suddenly, and she went a step nearer. "One good man has loved me, and I have loved a good man," she whispered; "for four' weeks life has been good." John Daere's face had grown dark. He had seen SOME thing of those four. weeks, of the in- fatuation of a young man—tind a rich young man—for a woman who was undoubtedly, an

adventuress. " icplain, Miss Murray, if you please," he said, coldly. She steadied her4elf and faced him. "When I leave the ship I shall not leave it in a boat," she said, abruptly', quite calmly. "I shall go down with it—with this ship—into the sea—to dream, When I gct into the boat I shall slip. But before I go I must confess—l must speak." Her voice shook, trembled uncertainly for a moment,- and was hoarse when she spoke again. "I want you to write something for me," she said., "There is no one els.?, no clergyman on board to, whom I ean speak; and I most speak; because you .will be saved; and you will take the message that—that will clear a man's name of a stain. You will do this for me? You will make a note of what I am going to say ? " Half bewildered he tore out a leaf from hie pocket-book and waited, pencil in hand. Her eyes, dark and haggard, stared at his hngers as though they mesmerised her, as though the. words she was about to speak were '-already- there, written in fire 'before her eyes. "Write,' she said, hoarsely. Write that • I —l—Olga, murdered Stephen Henderson, in Greatbridge Hall, six years ago, and that I ask forgiveness of Richard Sterry for the shadow of shame that has lain upon him all these years. Have you got that? Have you written that? He was suspected in my •place, but there was nothing—nothing to convict him, and the suspicion may have,clung to him all these years. But it will be all right now.' " The doctor stared aghast. His face had grown grey. He hesitated, then slowly "wrote, adding a few words of his own. "11 he pencil trembled in his hand as he handed it to her. " You—a murderess ! " he cried, under his breath. He passed his hand across his face "A murderess?" he repeated. She did not seem to hear. With set, .whita lips, with a sickening faintness upon her, she had signed her name below the words he had written, and looked .up. . "And you won't forget ? " she was Shying, breathlesrdy, " that you promise to keep this secret if you can clear Richard Sterry without. If you can—for heaven's sake let Sir Geoffrey believe me a good woman! Keep it from him if you can. I have loved him-so, and if Providence had given me another chance I should have been good to him, but He means me to die.
The accident which has disabled the ship is a 3ign. lam the Jonah on hoard, Dr. Daere. You will live, you will be saved, but Providence means me to die. The accident was a message, and
• oh I I shall be glad to die, for the burdon of it all these years has been heavy. Only now— only now—when Sir Geoffrey
She broke . off, looking round wildly at sea antl sky, turning her de3perate eyes to the s'un that -smiled back so cruelly. With a shudder 'she buried her face in her hands, and. .Dr.
)acre had no time to question her, for at that noment there came a sudden heavy lurching of he vessel, a sudden ominous trembling under- cut.

John nacre, thrown .lorward by the move- ment, reeled unsteadily and clutched at the rail. Olga Murray looked up: It's going," she said, huskily. " It's going!" A soda-water bottle rolled to the doctor's foot. He picked it up almost mechanically. Olga fell back and crouched down upon the deck. Higher up there was another desperate hurried movement to the boats. Women and children were thrust, in quickly, and the ropes loosened. The engines had-stopped long since, and now a sickening, suAing, gurgling. sound had .commenced. The water was coming in in elrnest now. It could no Ic.nger be kept out. It ran in, gurgling, chuckling: Women and children to the boats!" sang out a sailor's voice, and to them quickly, orderly, desperately, the women and children went. _

'Any more—any more Women and children?" sang the voice. The doctor, with his face hard- and his eyes steely, signed his name hastily as witness to the confession which he had written. She was a murderess—this beautiful woman—and it was his duty to bring her to justice if he could! Ile thrust the. paper into the bottle and look el up. . . Someone was running towar.:ls him over the shaking deck—a young Man with a hamlsome face grown white and haggard. The doctor stared dully at him, mechanically forcing a plus, of broken cork into the neck of the bottle. In that bottle \VIIS Olga Murray's confessien, and before him was the man who loved her! -Ile hesitated as if he would have spoken, but L. had not time. .

"1)r. Dacre,". Sir 'Geoffrey was' shouting, "where is Miss Murray? Where is she? She isn't in the boats--heavens! where can she be? Olga—Olga—darling!" The ship began to slip and roil heavily. One small boat put off into the open SO A. Another prepared to follow it, but suddenly, without warning, the g-eat ship gave a quick final lap to the sea, bearing over heavily to its swamping boats and human beings alike, thrust- ing them down, down into the se's cruel grasp. As it went, as it hee!ed over, Geoffrey, stumbling up, striking evt in a frantic effcrt to grasp at something, caught at a creuching figure on the deck.' " Olga!" he cried. "Olga—thank heaven!" He caught her to him. In the. mad terror and excitement of that moment he only temem- bored that he loved her—he forgot that he had known her only four short weeks—and with his arms round her, with his face upturned to the smiling sky, he sprang into the sea. As he did so. there went living nast his head

never • forget it, and neither will you, but all the same it will only be a dream; it will all go presently, and by-and ' we shall never believe that it was really you and I who lay on the deck side by side in the sun to get wog'. We shall never believe it, Geoffrey. It—it is begin- ning to fade already, that dream!" " Olga, my darling, you are talking nonsense. But I forgive you, little goose. Come here; I won't allotv you to hedge away. Here. I Say. .Now I have yon, and now—now—do you say this is a dream—this, darling? Am I only a phantom, or can you feel my flesh and bleed— re,' arms round you? Oh, my little girl—my wife as you will be soon—don't talk to me Of this dream fading ! It will never fade, dearest. I pray that we shall never—either of us—forget these last five days. They have given you te me. The wreck, the dip in the sea, that hor- rible moment I thought you were dead—oh! my sweet, ,it all only makes you more dear to me. And these last days when the sailors carried us up to lie on deck, and I could turn and see your dear face—Olga, my slveetheart, don't talk as if I should ever forget—as if it was a dream that would go. When you are my wife, when wC have settled down into. two re- spectable members of English seciety, when von and I. grow old and pr: .v and dull, I shall still remember this, my darling. I shall still see your face on my sheulder, with the salt water splashing it, I shall- still remember—more than C3II speak • of !" He caught her to him in a sudden convulsive clasp, and looked down at her white face. She had shut her eyes. She dared net look into his—she dared not think. It would be time enough to think when she saw England really before her—when the white cliffs steed out, when everything was at an end. But, mean- while, it wan so easy to -go on—it was such a wonderful dream. And she could. not put an end to it. She was not strong enough in the narrow compass of a ship. But when they reached land, and she could put a hundred miles between them, it would be different. She eould send him away then. She would make in go. But, meanwhile, she laved -him—ah ! -he loved him, and never in all her life had she hapov, never since her mother had died— aid surely she might get a little happiness, a ." days happiness, now? She looked up into his face and shrank a it was so blindly, wildly happy. Did he 'eve her as' much as that? • Would the parting be harder for him than she had thought? She looked round wilclly at sky and ocean. Suppose they did not -part after all—suppose she let him take her home to his mother? Who would ever know of the confession she had made? In Geoffrey's wife who would ever re- cognise the murderess? No one—surely no one? John Daere was dead. The ship which had picked up herself and Geoffrey had seen-no one else. John Dacre was dead—lying deep -underneath the great salt waves—And lying with him, with the water washinr, it clean, erasing it, destroying it, was the confession she had enade at that desperate moment. Why should- she not go on with Sir Geoffrey, why should she not become his wife? Why should she. not risk so little for, such a great reward? She clutched the rail so tiuhtiv that her

div.p: Tbere went flying past his head a bottle with a confession of murder in it 1

a bottle. It whizzed, sparkling green and gold in the sunlight—a soda-water bottle with a con- fessicn of murder in it ! " Olga shut her eyes and drew a sharp breath as they struck, water. It closed over them. They seemed to go down, down; they came up again, and always his arms were about, her tight, never loosening, never leaving her, and aiways there was that same light of love on his
The suli streamed down upon theli. She cßened her eyes. A few yards away, bobbing on the green water, flashing the light back to the, sun was that •bottle.
And on the horizon, steaming towards them, a

But when the sun went down that.night only two human beings were dragged from the grip of the sea—an unconscious woman and a man, who held her tightly clasped in his arms. He felt her lifted from him before exhaustion overtook him.

"Thank heaven I've saved yon, sweet!" he whispered, and then he, tee., was dragged .to safety. And on the sea th seda-water bottle still ducked and curtsied, and dipped—a tiny speck on the groat waste of water, bobbing and sidling a 3 it was washed away from the wreck.

hands grew cold° and numb, and her fingers seemed frozen. Into her eyes had come a sudden passionate longing. She loved him so r She faced him slowly, making one last effort to set him free. "No, no! We shall remem- ber," she said, "but—we must remember apart."

"Olga -7=P "No, no; listen!" She - looked •up, her breath coming thick and ,fast. "You cannot marry me. You had not seen me a month ago, and, even though we have been through so much together, what do you know of me? That I had been out to Australia as governess, that I was going back to England to try to get a situation there. -What more do you know? What more can you find out? And you—Sir Geoffrey Verriker—you muit have a wife above—above suspicion—not. me, Geoffrey, not me." " Rubbish, darling ! I shall have the wife I loyeVaid you are she. I only care for you— for your face, which is honest and true, and your eyes, which are brave, and your lips, which cannot lie. Olga, you need not try to frighten me. Nothing you can say will make me give you uy except—except that you don't love me. And yAn can't say that, Olga." . .

She oould not. She turned away again, and before her, on that sunny day, a shadow swept acrcss the sea, turning it cold for her, cold and grey, and black. " can't—l mustn't marry you ! " she cried, with a sob.

"Tell me why? I know you love me, and you can't find any reason for refusing to marry me, sweetheart. I know enough of you, and I know I love you as I never loved another woman, and that.is enough for me." "But—but you are rich, and a big man," she faltered.

He laughed. "Yes, and six weeks ago I was as big a nobody as you," he cried. "Six or eight weeks ago I was hard at work on a ranch, while you .were governess to a fine, young English lady of title! Oh, yes, • I see . What it is, yqu are too gcod for me, and too polite to tell me so out- right. What is a mere baronet? Eh? Olga, I won't hear of such nonsense. I shall take you straight home with me, and introduce you to my mother and sister. „They will be waiting at Komscote Hall for me—that's the name of my place; as I told you-and there you.and I will .g 3 together—you and I! We shall see the old place together, side by side. I have almost forgotten what it is like, for J 7 was .a small boy when -I saw it last, and I nev r expected to in- herit--my uncle hated my father too much.' He was-in love with my mother, and never iorgave her or my father for marrying, and Ile always meant to leave the money away from me. But he didn't, after all. He couldn't rob me of the title, but the estate would have been hopeless without the money, and that I have got, it after all is the strangest accident. He was going to marry a. widow, and died only a few weeks before the wedaing—hard lines on her." He stood silent -for a minute, frowning at some,recollection, and then went on, lightly: " My mother will be pleased, and Ethel— my little sister—will have a chance now, thank goodness ! I tell you, Olga, ' you've nothing to grumble about in the way of our greatness. My mother was poor enough even for you to anurove of six months ago.. and - there was

every 'prospect of Ethel going out governessing like yourself. So there, miss! Now for the next objection?" He looked down at her smiling, dreaming nothing, suspecting nothing, and she looked back at.him with her heart beating fit to break, with a pain almost too bitter to be borne. She looked back at sea and sky. Why not? Why not risk it? On a sudden, far off, there appeared on the horizon a fine line of white. " England !" she cried, He put his arm round her. "Home, my darl- ing," he said. •

div.head: CHAPTER 11.
div.p: CHAPTER 11.

Five days later the sun shone still as though no tragedy had taken place, as though the blue sea held nothing ugly beneath its, smiling breast. The weather held, and a-s the ship ap- -.3.7.ed England it seemeJ as if it. was giv- ir_i; them all a vvelcome—ealling them " heire." Olga stood quite still, grasping in her nerve- less fingers the cold •iron rail of the deck, with her eyes staring out—staring ,always straight before her—at .the dim far line of ocean, where presently would appear a streak of white—in- d,stinct at first, but gradually changing and brightening, until at last it would resolve itself into a shining line of cliiis—England! Sir Geoffrey 'Verricker stood beside her; but he had no eyes for Englamt no thoughts for " home," no thoughts for anyone just then except for the girl he had sti,e(.l: from the sca— the girl he loved—the girl he had not known a month ago. - He put out his hand and 'touched hers.. _ .
"Olga," h. said, "Nvhat are /you 'thinking of?"
" I was thinking," she said, -" that—that it will not be long now. The end is upon ..us— almost."

"The end? What end? Olgac don't talk like that. There can be no end now—for you and me. Only one thing can take you from me now, my sweetheart, and that is death ; and that. we no longer fear, darling, for we have faced it together—you and I. Olga," he paused for a minute, taking her hand in his, .anaViving one glance away from her set face to the dim horizon beyond which lay England, "Olga darling, I shall take you straight to my mother —straight as we can go, clearest, you and I." "No, no," she shrank away, dragging her hand from his grasp, facing him wildly. " Geoffrey—oh ! Geoffrey, we have had a beautiful, wonderful, mad week—this last week —but it must come to an end soon now. It has been a dream. Geoffrey—no more. I shall

"Well?" Mrs., Dunston raised herself from \ner couch with au impatient movement. " Well, Julia, is there any news ? "
_ "No, none," sfie aid. "The boat is three days late now, and no elle knows what has become of it. It may be—it may be at the bottom of the sea." _ _

Mrs. Dunston.drummed with her slender white fingers on the table before her. Her face grew bard and sot, and the jewels on her fingers flashed sharply in the sunlight. She had once been a beautiful woman, but now her thin, wan face shewed only the remnants of her beauty. The bright eyes were there, the rich crown of golden-red hair was there, and the -straight white brow was there, but underneath them all was a tired, fretful face, with lines, fine as a spider's web, shewing underneath the rouge and powder, with deep furrows running down between nose and mouth. Mrs Dunston had a gambler's mouth—the fight,- fixed,. yet nervous lips of a pers:n who stakes his life cn a throw.

Yet, perhaps, in spite of all that she would have still been accounted a beautiful woman if her daughter Julia had not been present. But beside her daughter, Mrs. Dunston looked a veritable rag, washed out, pallid, ashen, insipid ; and Julia, with: her bright red hair and beau- tiful face, with her straight dark brows, and curved red lips, with her brown eyes, with occasionally a hint of red in them, and her full white throat, made the older wuman insigni- ficant, small, and trifling. Her fingers ceased to drum for a moment. "He ,nut come home ! " she said, harshly. " Fate'. will not play us another trick. The boat is only delayed—it will arrive- all right." Julia went over to the window and looked out. .
—" But if it does not?" she said. Geoffrey does not come?"
" Supposo

Mrs. Dunston gave her. •daughter a quick glance, but Julia's face was, turned away. But perhaps she guessed how ashen her cheeks were, and that her strained eyes saw nothing of the summer sky outside. She 'hesitated a moment,. Then: "You hay.:ni!t, got over the old infatuation? " she asked, a little harshly. "Why. can't you forget Geoffrey Verriker? If .he is at the bottom of the sea, whet then? His cousin Edward will inherit ; and Edward—Edward "—she rose from the couch and turned slowly, with a strange; sinuous movement, towards her daughter— Edward would do murder for you if you asked him," she whispered, harshly. "Julia, why you are a fool? Fate has played me a shabby trick, but you must not fail. In three weeks "-- she clenched her hards—" I should have been Lady Verriker,. and all that yonder—all that great park, the house—it would litave been all mine—all mine !' Julia, it makes me desperate to think of it—to see it slipping from nae—to see that white old woman and a chit of a girl like Ethel Verriker there where you should he! Oh, we must get it back, we must turn them out—.. somehow—,somehow !, And if Geoffrey is at the bottom or the sea—you must marry Edward, Julia!" _ _ .

Julia stood rigid, staring blindly before her at the gorgeous summer, day. Her hands. stretched out to the window panes, grew cold and still. From somewhere deep down in her heart came a passionate cry—" Geoffrey!" Her mother stood close beside her. " I almost believe it would be a good thing if Geoffrey was at the bottom of the sea," she said, harshly— "for he never loved you; and Edward—" _ _

Julia swung round,. her eyes were blazing, her breath came quickly., " Oh, I hate.him—l hate him!" she cried. " Sometimes I scarcely know which'l hate most, him or Edward. But—but whether he is alive or dead, I—l will be Lady Verriker, mother !"

. Mrs. Dunston fell back with a strange, bitter smile upon her lips. If she had one weak spot in her heart—if she bad any heart at all—it was for her daughter Julia. Yet, for a moment, the thought of how close she herself had been to the title brought a deep line about her set lips and a wave of White across her cheeks. _

" Yes—yes," she said, hastily. "We must get the title—you and I ! I have failed "—she laughed harshly—" and it is your turn now, and if Geoffrey does not come back there is Edward madly in love yith you." _ _ _ _

Julia 'shivered suddenly. Heartless and am- bitious though she was, yet the thought of Edward Verriker unnerved her. And she loved Geoffrey! She stood swinging the blind to and fro, staring out at the dazzling sunshine, thinking how a few months ago she had cheated herself into the belief that he had loved her. Loved her! A flush of rage rose to her cheeks. He :had never loved her, and she had been mad.. Her mother had said so, and she admitted it now. If he had so much as held out a finger to her she would have forgotten everything for hint—would have shared poverty, hardships, Misery with him—thrown all he ambition to the winds and gone with him across the seas to anything. But he had gone, unthinking and careless, without. a sigh for her. Now she laughed scorn- fully to herself, and said he did not know what love was, and if he ever came back he would find her different. She was learning to hate him. She might hate him, even though she was ready to marry him. And if he would not marry her—well, there was Edward—Edward, who was 'ready to do murder for her! She repeated her words sharply: Lady Verriker, mother!" , (To be continued.)

The net profits of the Union Bqnk of Manchester, Limited, for the half-ycar cnded 30th June, including £10,057 brought forward, amount to £47,240. The Directors have declared the usual dividend of 12s. per share (free of Income Tax) absorbing £30,000, and have transferred £2,500 to Premises Reduction Account, £2,000 to Pension Fund, and £5,C00 to Reserve Fund raising that fund to £360,000), leaving the amount to be carried forward, £7:740.
[By Redcap.] - THE SUSSEX SYSTEM OF FATTENING
When I speak of the Sussex system it must not be inderstood that it is in this county alone where )oultry fattening is a large industry. This special

branch of poultry— culture—has of recent -years grown tremendously in other parts of the country ; but we owe to the Surrey and Sussex farmers and dealers (especially) very much indeed for the introduction of the best methods in the art of fattening and dressing poultry for the market. They use the same breeds and crossbreeds as others yet none can beat them. The Sussex fatters seem to possess a kind of inherited instinct which tells them exactly when a bird is doing either well or ill and therefore they act accordingly with a fair share of success. And, because of such experience,we naturally bow to the Sussex fatters and adopt their methods, improving or altering, as condi- tions demand.
FATTENING COOPS,
There are many methods adopted in fattening poultry. Two however .are specially .recommended and these

I shall deal with, vi : Trough feeding from cages or coops and cramming. These coops are constructed and arranged in single rows about three feet from the ground. The size of each pen should be three feet long and about 18 inches wide and the same height. In each pen of these dimensions you could accom- modate six fowls of a good size. Of course the pens should be constructed of open woodwork so as to admit of a constant current of f-esh air, not only so

but the 'floor of the pen would be kept free from dirt. So much the better if the cross bars on the bottom of of the pens are round ; then the droppings much more' easily fall through. A trough should be placed along the front of the pens from which the birds feed through the open wood-work. It is essential that such a row of pens be placed in a quiet spot as quiet- -ness is conducive to quick feeding. The attendant should always be on the alert and any bird of a fighting character should be removed and plac,ed in a

pen by „itself. • Sometimes a whole lot. of fowls are upset by the quarrelsome nature of one or two. In fact it is of the greatest importance that fowls that are being so treated should be kept quiet and peaceful.
FOODS AND FEEDING

The young birds should be placed in the pens -when about three months old. They should be made to fast for about 12 hours after being placed in the coops, so that you will be sure the first meal will be eaten greedily. Thus you have taken the first step towards making them content. They should be fed twice daily, say about 6 a.m. and 7 p.m. during the summer season. If. this is an inconvenient time fix your own. But remember that whatever times for feed-

ing you may happen to fix, you must rigidly adhere to. This is very important, because by so doing the fowls are always ready for the meal when the time comes round. Some people say that two meals a day are not sufficient. They seem to forget that fowls so confined have not an opportunity of running the flesh off their bones. I recommend my readers to stick to the lines suggested for the simple reason, that if you feed too often the birds will get sick of seeing the food, and consequently will not fatten near so quickly. The food should consist of ground oats and a small percentage of barley meal and middlings or thirds, mixed. together with milk. The food should be given soft or about the consistency of oat-meal porridge. The milk used should be sour, as it has been found that if so used it takes the place of vegetable food as a corrective for the bowels. Milk also is a valuable fattening food and adds very much to the whiteness of the flesh. It may seem to some people that such a diet would be found expensive, . _ .

especially seeing that milk is recommended. This is not so if the following advice be adopted :—Get a large vessel to hold, say, about three gallons of liquid. Then pu-chase skimmed or separ-ated milk, and add one quart of new milk to every tt.Jquarts of skimmed, allow it to go sour and constantly renew the supply by frequent-additions in the manner suggested. Do not forget that if proper attention is paid to your stock, about three weeks„ of such treatment will suffice in getting them ready for market. So taking everything into due consideration the expense does not last long, and you will be amply repaid by better prices than if they were fed haphazard.

div.head: CRAM M ING
div.p: CRAM M ING

is another method of fattening poultry'. This system is carried out by using what is called a cramming machine. In appearance it resembles a coffee-mill, save for the tube and treadle. A rubber tube is

passed into the bird's mouth which, being held by the attendant, is fed artificially by forcing the food through the tube by pressing down a foot treadle which is connected with the upper part of the machine. Now to successfully cram a bird is very difficult and it needs considerable experience to become efficient. Great care has to be taken not to

either over-feed or underfeed a fowl. Experi- enced hands can tell directly by feeling the bird's crop when sufficient food . has been administered and in this lies the secret of the whde business. I should advise anyone who intended going in for poultry fattening as a special branch, to spend some little time under the tuition of an experienced poultry fatter. This would always pay you as the risk in the loss of birds would be diminished as a result. The cost of a cramming machine generally runs from two to three pounds and can be recommended at this figure.
HAND CRAMMING

is another method and a good one. To me it seems more humane than machine cramming, and yet there is no pain attached to the latter system. Both methods are good but band-Cramming could be resorted to where the number of birds was not large. The same directions could be followed with equally good results, as those recommended last week for fattening turkeys. The same food also as that in trough feeding but given not quite so sloppy. In fact, you could not administer the food very) well unless sufficiently stiff to make into pellets or small balls. This method may be found somewhat tedious, but it will repay you for the extra trouble, as some of the very finest table specimens are thus produced. ,1 bad almost forgotten to mention that absolute cleanliness must, prevail. See that all utensils are kept clean, and give an occasional limewash to the cpops.

• GENERAL OBiERVATIOKS soon show what particular class of fowls are demanded. In some of our largest •markets high price's are paid for very young chickens. In the No: th of England, however, we have to cater for a more industrial class of people, and while perhaps price is not altogether the object, quantity must at the same time prevail. It is of very little use to offer a couple of chickens about the size of pigeons to the housewife of a Lancashire cotton operative. What I want to point out is this : that to ;nyone engaged in the poultry farming industry a good opening for large well-fed table fowls presents itself. There is, especially at this season of the year,a vast demarid for them in sea-side !laces, and the enterprising fatter should reap a good return. I hope the time will soon • come when we shall see • less of the scrappy, pigeon-breasted specimens -hanging on our market stalls and in poultry shop windows. The remedy for lack of interest in scientific and practical poultry farming., is now, I am pleased to say, largely being found 1; a closer perusal of theories based upon practical experi- ence. I hope my readers will give closer attention to , this side of poultry farming. What 'they have • been doing in the Southern counties (for one Might almost say ages) might have been more extensively done in the North. The demand is enormous and if it were not for the excessive price of land, I feel sure that it

The Examiner, Saturday, July 10, 1909

immense success. The united procession was one of the largest ever seen in Warrington. I was also successful in establishing for a number QK years an annual musical festival in the Public Hall (now the Court Theatre), when the combined choirs under the leader- ship of Mr. T. Mee Pattison, gave services of sacred music. I much regret that this annual event,. which was financially and numerically successful, has not yet been attempted in 'Parr Hall.

It is generally known that I have always taken a very deep interest iu every move- ment for the promotion of temperance. As a boy I attended open-air meetings at Bridge Foot. Nearly all the Temperance worthies of 40 years ago were known to me. The names of Richard Home, William Gregson, George F. Podmore, George Lomax. Thomas Whittaker, Simeon Smithard, Edward Grubb, Thomas Hardy, J. H. Raper, Dr. Lees, James Teare and William Mee will be familar to many. I knew them all, and was proud to serve under their leadership, and by my life and work imitate their example of self-denial for the good of others. This early training stimulated me in temperance work. The old Temperance Society, the Temper- ance Union and the Temperance Federation I was for many years the honorary secretary of and for a great number of years I was responsible for organising opposition to appli- cations for new licenses at the annual Brewster Sessions.

I Many years ago at the Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay, along with Thomas Dale, Thomas Ashley and a few others I assisted in starting the Warrington Band of Hope Union and for some years was chair- man and secretary of the committee which successfully carried out the annual procession and gala. During the past thirty years almost all the great temperance demonstra- tions held in Warrington I have organised and carried out with the assistance of volun- tary helpers and have received the personal congratulations of the late Cardinal Manning

some stirring l scenes. I -vrell remember Mottram's-yardz. and Nomination Day in' the Fair Ground, when Sir Richard Cross and the late Mr. Samuel Rigby strongly Opposed each other upon the hustings. I was a messenger on 'the Election day in the memorable South-East Ward when the unfortunate blunder occurred which gave the seat to Mr. Rylands. As Liberals we went home to bed the defeated party, and at midnight a cry arose that Rylands was in. We all got up and, amid the roar of cannons and the ringing of works' bells we celebrated the Liberal victory of 1868. From then, until recently, I have taken a very active part in every Parliamentary contest. I have served the party at the local headquarters for a great number of years. I have many amusing recollections of the 1880 election when Mr. McMinnies gained so notable a victory, which I cannot here relate. The contests in the County Divisions in which Warrington was a part I assisted in, and I remember upon one occasion taking a cab for a voter who was of large proportions. When I arrived with the cab I could not get him into it, so had to return with an open carriage. I then managed to push him• in sideways and rode with him in triumph to Grappenhall school. Upon our arrival at the entrance, surrounded by the leaders of both parties,my voter could not get out of the carriage, and whether he had grown on the journey I can- not say but amidst the cheers and laughter of the crowd and the language of my voter which was more expressive than polite, I drove him into a side lane and eventually succeeded in getting him out and polling his vote. In municipal elections I have had charge of many contests. I served the party as chairman of North-West Ward when a memorable contest was fought between Samuel Beaman and John Roberts and my man won handsomely. After this victory I was asked to become Chairman of Orford Ward and occupied this

div.head: SCENE IMMEDIATELY AFTER THE DISASTER.
div.p: THE SCENE IMMEDIATELY AFTER THE DISASTER.

The trench disaster at Newport, Mon., recalls in many ways the recent accident at the Victoria Dock, Birkenhead. Three minutes before the men were due to cease work for the day a deep trench collapsed and sixty-six men were buried under a mass of falling timbers. Gallant rescue work enabled some of the imprisoned men to make their escape, but the death-roll was ultimately found to be over thirty. The water from the river made its way into the trench and rose to a height considerably above the level at which the men were working, so that the poor fellows who were not killed outright by the debris must have met their death by drowning. Magnificent heroism was shown by the rescuers, one of whom, Tom Lewis, sixteen years of age, worked for two hours, head downwards, in an unsuc- cessful effort to release an imprisoned comrade.

div.head: W. T. WILLIAMS, White *ouse,
div.p: W. T. WILLIAMS, White *ouse,
SANKEY STREET, Warrington.

the late Sir Wilfrid Lawson, the late Rev. Charles Garrett,the late J. H. Raper, the late W.S. Caine, M.P., the Dean of Hereford, the Dean of Carlisle,Rev.Canon Hicks, and many other distinguished men. Thirty-five years ago, mainly through the efforts of Mrs. Reaney, supported by Alder- man William Nield, Mr. Thomas Morris, and my brother, Mr. Henry Roberts, I assisted in the formation of the Warrington British Workman Public-house Company, Ltd. This Company has been one of the most suc- cessful of. its kind in the country, having been conducted upon strict business lines,and
has returned in dividends to the shareholders double the amount of its capital. Nine years ago some of us, impressed with

the absolute necessity of providing a high class cafe in Warrington,determined to make the attempt. My brother Mr. F. R. Roberts took the initiative and with the valued assistance of the late Mr. Henry Milling, Mr. Walter Brough,Mr. J. W. Hayward and Mr. John Hesketh succeeded in forming a local. company. The Winmarleigh Cafe was opened, and under the capable ' management of Mrs. Hayward was immediately a great success and still continues to maintain its high reputation. A second, the King's Cafe, Bridge-street, has since been opened and has also been quite successful. I have been the secretary of this company since its formation. and I honestly believe I have done more for the Temperance cause by assisting in the establishment of these cafes than all the meetings I have ever attended. The results have been eminently satisfactory both morally, socially and financially. It would seem strange if I concluded this narrative without some reference_ to my
political career. In the year 1868 I went to every political meeting both outdoor and indoor in support of the late Mr. Peter
Rylands. I enjoyed myself immensely attending those meetings.Th.e campaign corn-

meneed in Cairo-street schools- until the room was far too small. I remember the late William Diggle, ot water fame, taking upon himself the duties of doorkeeper and upon several occasions when I sought admis- sion to the meeting he refused to let me in remarking" they had no room for lads." I got in, however,notwithstanding Mr. Diggle's opposition. I had a great admiration for Mr. Rylands as a speaker and it is a curious fact that his addresses made a Liberal of me, and at any i ate gave me my political education, and when I read the speeches of Mr. W.Peter. Rylands, the present chairman of our local Conservative party, I remember that his father taught me my political faith which still remains unchanged. During that memorable election I witnessed

position for some years and retired with all the seats filled by Liberals. I then returned to the ward where I resided "St. Austin's Ward" and was elected its Chairman along with Alderman Tinnion. Our first election upon the extension of the Ward resulted in the election of three Liberals. And now I must conclude. After working hard for others for a great number of years I was asked to enter the Council eight years ago. I accepted and was elected without a contest. I entered the Council with an earnest desire to serve the town I was born in to the very best of my ability. I faithfully and conscientiously discharged those duties for three years. Circumstances which I will not repeat,as they are well-kno wn,compelled my retirement as an honourable man. This experience has not been without its consola- tions and its reward. I determined to retire into private life and withdrew from many associations I had been actively engaged in. I took up my residence near Grappenhall intending to carry out my fixed detel mination of complete retirement. Very soon after, to my complete surprise, a Conservative Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster offered to appoint me a magistrate for the borough. This appreciation from my political opponents of my services to my native town, touched me more deeply than anything I had ever previously experienced. It came to me at a moment in my life when I least expected it and from those upon whose favour I had no claim. I accepted the posi- tion and determined that I had still some work to do for Warrington, and mlust do my duty without fear or favour. Like others, I have had my joys and sorrows, and now as I reflect upon the past I remember with gratitude that in all my public work I have been encouraged and helped by my devoted wife who, amidst great bodily affliction, struggled with a family of little ones, when duty required my absence from home almost every night during a long period of years. And now in closing may I add that the Liberalism of Cobden, Gladstone and Bright is still my political faith and"peace retrench- ment and reform" my motto. As the years advance my temperance principles are stronger with ripened experience and my heart is saddened almost daily by• personal corttact with those who are the victims of excess. I have hope for the future and still believe that a victory is yet within sight, and that the clouds of Intemperance which have so long darkened our skies will be scattered by the golden beams of Truth and Temperance.

This was the 'first occasio lon which a reigning monarch had visited Rugby, and the town c'id honour to the notable event by gaily decorating its sti eets and building. Our illustration shows the King planting an oak tree in the school close. Beside him is Dr. H. A. James, the headmaster.

div.head: GROWING TURKEYS.
div.p: GROWING TURKEYS.

Full liberty should be allowed the growing poultry stock, as they cannot thrive in confinement, points out "Farm and Home." If they have access to good pasture or arable land, healthy goslings and turkey chickens should be able to find half their own living during the next few weeks. Many turkeys will pass through the critical stage of " shooting the red " this mouth; which takes piaci, when they are about eight weeks old. During the few days the red is making its appearance, the birds require extremely careful treat- ment. They must not be allowed on to wet grass, they must be protected from rain and too much sun, and they must be liberally fed upon nourishing foods.
COMMERCIAL FAlLURES.—According to " Kemp's Mercantile Gazette," the total number of Commercial _

Failures recorded in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, July 2nd, was 151, viz. :—New Bankruptcy Proceedings published in the London Gazette, 75 ; Deeds of Arrangement registered, 76. The respective numbers in the corresponding week of last year : Bankruptcies, 78; Deeds of Arrangement, 64—Total 142; being an increase of 9. The total number of Commercial Failures recoried during the 27 weeks of the present year is 4,200 ; the total number recorded in the corresponding 27 weeks of last year was 4,399, showing a decrease of 199.

The Princesses of Fife.—Contrary to expectation, Princess Alexandra of Fife has appeared at very few functions this season. Like her Royal mother, Princess Alexandra has no great love for "strangers," and much prefers her happy and somewhat secluded home life to the whirl of society. The young Princess, who is very pretty, greatly resembles her grandmother the Queen, and her intense love for yachting and the sea dates almost from babyhood. It may be doubted if the young Princesses a Fife—who are both very shy and reserved, will ever appear in Society as the Princess Patrica of Connaught has done,going hither and thither,visiting and travelling, with only a lady-in-waiting in attendance. Royal v isiters.—Princess Frederick Charles of Hesse- Cassel, who with her children is making a three-weeks stay in this country, is the youngest of the German Emperor's three sisters. Her husband. a Prince of Hesse-Cassel, which was annexed to Prussia in 1866, is very rich, and the Princess has on several occasions entertained her uncle, King Edward, at the palace of Cronberg, near Homburg, which belonged to the late Empress Frederick. Among Royal guests who are expected to pay our Court a visit this summer, are also the German L:rown Prince and Princess. It will be the Princess's first visit, but the Crown Prince has been here before, and some few years ago he stayed a fort- night,.paying a round of private visits, being the guest oi the Duke and Duchess of Sutherland at Dunrobin Castle, of Lord Rosebery, at Dalmeny, and of the Duke of Marlborough at Blenheim. He is supposed to share the friendly regard for this country which distinguished his grandparents, the late Emperor and Empress Frederick, a sentiment which unfortunately, as before, is not very popular with the German people. Women's Subjection.—Miss Cecily Hamilton, in her newly-published book "Marriage as a Trade" deals with the social and economic independence of women from various points of view, but the one broad fact which stands out in discussion of this kind, is that since the mid-Victorian period, women have largely attained to a mental equality with men. Women students at Cambridge have been placed "equal to" and "above the Senior Wrangler,' and who can tell what the world nits lost by the past system of holding women back from culture and high intellectual attainments. Still it is no longer necessary for a women to marry " for a living," and that has to a great extent, relieved her from a position of servitude. One knows that in these days when money is everything, the typical parent says to the average girl "marry means and a position, that will 'remain when youth and sentiment are gone," and in that sense marriage is, and always has been, something of a trade. But the days when no self-respecting woman could maintain herself, except as the appanage of a husband, are gone. Almost every conceivable kind of occupation is open to her, and one inevitable result is, that women are less inclined to marry on the old con- ditions of servitude which men with their chivalry, their physical and mental superiority, have in the past ex.cted from them.

The Art of Servant Keeping.—One not infrequently hears the remark that the better you treat your servants the worse they treat you, and vics versa. That, how- ever, like many trite sayings, lacks truth, and where it is heard one generally Ilncrs that it means the chronic state of things of discharging one bad servant and awaiting the advent of worse. Housewives who act on such principles will not keep a good servant if one happens to come their way. Provided one has a com- petent and •capable person to deal with, the art of servant keeping is to make her responsible fot the carrying out ot her duties, to leave her alone, and accord her some of the liberty and freedom she would have if she went out to business. In very many cases the business girl works harder than the house servant, but after hours her time is her own, and she is free to wear a large hat, and occupy herself with matters of dress and her outings. Mrs. Carey in a little book on the Domestic Servant problem, suggests recourse to Norwegian and Scandinavian girls, for whom there is an agency at East Orinstead. They are quiet, hard-work- ing, domesticated girls, are more than content with the wages they receive, and have none of that repugnance for domestic service which is so prevalent among girls in this country. Sale Time.—" Scrimmages" at the sales are grow- ing more and more pronounced as the years go on, and not a few women who have every right to lay claim to the title of" gentlewoman," nowadays behave at a sale very like our unfortunate sisters in the slums, when they happen to be displeased with one another or- the militant Suffragists. Indeed what with the feeling that detectives are closely watching the excited customers and that any moment a battle between the said customers may ensue, sale time and especially Remnant Days in large emporiums are often decidedly tiling to those women who desire to maintain their dignity and reputation for good manners. Changes Coming.—Ourskirts,so say authorities on the subjeet,are shortly to widen and flow out,and our hats will grow smaller, and soon instead of looking like a huge mushroom on a stalk,we shall rather lean to the balloon with a little knot on top. Of course there is no chance of a revival of the crinoline, but full and flow- ing skirts are surely "arriving," also the small hat. Consequently heaagear trimmed and untrimmed is going very chenplj at the sales, also made-up, and unmade robes, aud I rovided we are prepared to wear them and promptly. such purchases should indeed prove a delight to the thrifty bargain hunter. Princess Slips.—The home art ssmalier has her task made more and more easy every season,and especially is mis the case just now, when in addition to the delight- ful ready-made " blouse-suits " in linen, cotton and muslin ready-to-wear Princess slips of white batiste, provided with long sleeves and a kilted frill at the hem, are being offered for a few shillings in shopland. Moreover these slips ate made in different sizes and lengths, so that little alteration is generally necessary. The Bolero.—Half-a-dozen years ago our toilet was complete without a bolero. It is therefore not a matter for surprise thas we became tired of it, and left it for a time severely alone. Next we took a violent fancy . to emulate this little garment, by-means of braiding and embroideries, and now its time has come again, and it will shortly be" the vogue." Few will raise any protest to this move on the part of Dame Fashion, for the bolero properly cut and built is becoming to all, old and young, stout and slender alike. Cheap Editions.—Publishers and authors are once more lamenting that they have fallen upon evil days. The public will not buy the six-shilling novel, and there is no doubt that the quick reprint in cheap editions has helped to kill the sale of the higher priced article. The public will not buy the 6s. book when it can be had some titne hence for sevenpence, and with few exceptions publishers and authors are agreed that that means starvation for them, and the final extinction of good literature. It is true that people will not pay more for a book than they need pay, but the new enter- prise of cheap editions is not the only cause of the decline of the 6s. novel. One is never so uncertain of getting value for money as when buying a book, and the over production of worthless novels has made the public distrustful, both as regards quantity and quality. Sometimes books are artificially spun out to bulk between the covers, but there is no differentation in price bother it is a long or short story. Moreover the reading public has learnt to like the cheap reprint not only on account of its being cheap, but because it is only novels that have merit and command an immense dale which can possibly pay to issue in this form. -

div.head: HUI TIP. JUNG CAME TO WARRINGTON. –
div.p: HUI TIP. JUNG CAME TO WARRINGTON. -
[With apologies to Mr. Arthur Bennett.]

Oh who will forget the glorious Gth,- The day when the King came hither, When this ancient town was upside down And loyal hearts a-dither ! The streets were alight with pennons bright, When the King and th. 3 Queen rode hither. " We shall not soon forget the day When they rode here together."

Little we reeked of the waiting hours For the King and the Queen were coining, And we left our toil for the glad turmoil With which the streets were humming; - We were going to see his Majesty In royal sunny weather. "We shall not sothilorget the day When they rode here together." But hush, .they are coming ; from far and wide We hear thedistant.cheering, And we're longing to add our voices glad When the King comes within bearing, And we'll see the grace in the Queen's sweet face When the royal ear conies hither. The King and Queen shall never forget . When they rode here together.

And see they come. Five noble steeds ; • - Appear and are lost to vision. Then some motors whizz by,,and in vain we try To catclitlie sight elysian, And pale as death, we hold our breath In spite of the golden weather., "We shall not soon forget the day When they rode here together." , .

For the royal car had sped afar While we a cheer were raising, But never a glimpse of the King or Queen Did .we gather for all our gazing. They had come and gone, while we looked on In the golden sunny weather. . "We shall not soon forget the day When they rode here together. '

'Did you.see the King? Did you see the Queen? ' Cried everyone together, But eyes just bright had lest their light In spite of the sunny weather ; Our banners seemel tarnished and turned to. grey, . Our garlands seMied to wither. Oh, we shall not soon forget the day When the King and Quten came hither. July 6th, 19)9

div.head: THREE MONTHS IN INDIA, SYRIA, AND PALESTINE.
div.p: THREE MONTHS IN INDIA, SYRIA, AND PALESTINE.
By Truda H. Crosfield.

div.head: (ARTICLE I.)
div.p: (ARTICLE I.)

Having been invited to contribute to the "Examiner" an account of the tour I made in India, Syria and Palestine this winter, I have much pleasure in doing so, but must apologise for the desultory jottings which result. It is delightful to run over all one saw and experienced in that .vast old world of the East; but if statistics and political information are expected I am afraid they will not be found. These weighty and con- flictipg matters are ready to hand in many a book, pamphlet and leading article. To attempt to sum up an opinion during a short three months' visit during which one heard different opinions in different quarters would have been foolish. I will content myself therefore with a description of travel and scenery, which I hope readers of the " Examiner " will find of some interest.

Miss Benson and myself joined the P. and 0. s.s. " Syria " at Marseilles on the 22nd November, 1908. We took the overland route in order to escape the Bay of Biscay, as Miss Benson entirely crumples up on the sea. In this we were justified, for the voyage had been rough, but from Marseilles onward the sea was calm as a river. None the less, as we emerged from dinner on the first evening our steward informed ,us that a " fo!lowing " wave had quietly washed in at our port-hole and flooded our cabin! Luckily,Our dresses were all hanging on pegs forward of the porthole, and escaped, and only a few shoes got sopped. But how it came in on such a calm evening has for ever

who came to trade ostrich feathers and other produce, and who are apparently childishly vain. They wash their woolly hair, with lime I believe; anyway, it turns to a gorgeous red-gold shade; and they wear it stiffened and erect six inches abbve their head, which makes them lobk exactly like gollywogs. With their glorious white teeth, rolling agate eyes and cheerful grins, they are remarkable looking people. It was after Aden that deck games began. Why the hottest week of the voyage should ,have been selected for competitions and gnyn-ikhana, I do not know. , Perhaps it was to leave us time to practise beforehand. Anyhow, we all now set to with desperate earnestness at "Buckets," " Bullboard," " Shuffleboard " and "Quoits." Deck quoits is a grand game and gives you some exercise. It is played on the principle of bowls, with rope rings, and it is not the easiest thing to knock out other quoits when the ship is swaying; but shuffleboard, or deck billiards, is in my opinion worthy to be the invention of the evil one. You " shuffle " small wooden discs, by means of a staff, a distance of 20 feet or so along the deck. The object is to lie in the centre of two chalked rings, and each player has three discs and many turns. I had seven turns and never got a disc to stay in, where- upon I abandoned shuffleboard for ever. Miss Benson, however, won first prize for it, and as I got the same for quoits and buckets, there was much jubilation at our table. On leaving Marseilles.

div.head: MISS CROSFIELD AND MISS BENSON AT MOUNT LAVINIA, CEYLON.
div.p: MISS CROSFIELD AND MISS BENSON AT MOUNT LAVINIA, CEYLON.

remained a mystery. We passed Messina, looking transparently beautiful in the clear Italian morning light. The sea was a turquoise green colour, the precipitous mountains of Sicily, rose-brown near at hank faded to violet in the distance, and further down the steep coasts towered the immense white dome of Etna. We little thought how ghastly a ruin wduld befall those white houses ere we steamed past them six months later.

we had said to each other 'Whatever shall we do during twenty-seven days at sea, mostly out of sight of land,' and had solemnly laid in a store of books. It i§ an amazing fact that we each of us barely finished read- ing one in the time. Between deck games, bridge drives, music, conversation and letters home, the daily round on ship board fills up amazingly. We were a small number on the" Syria," and in tbe course of a fortnight had •become like one large family. It -was delightful to see elderly couples playing in the competitions with the earnestness of school children. One old general had to be led away to the other side of the deck when his wife was playing the final in buckets, the intensity of his excitement so upset her, besides being bad for him ! We passed the great island of Socotra, its mountains wrapped in cloud, and the next land sighted was a regular tropical coral island. It was dream-like to watch the lazy green billows breaking on the reefs, the dense growth of palms and cocoanut trees down to the shore, the black skinned natives fishing in the still, green lagoon, and the bright birds flitting in the branches. One's childish imaginations, drawn from the Swiss Family. Robinson, an):1 Coral Island, had come true. The next morning we awoke to find ourselves anchored in Columbo.

div.head: THROUGH THE GREAT CANAL.
div.p: THROUGH THE GREAT CANAL.

It was at sunset, twb days after, that we saw the low line of Port Said rising to star- board. The African shore is so flat that the houses at first appear to be standing in the sea. Everyone crowded to gaze at the long breakwater, on which stands the statue of deLesseps,his arm extended as though invit- ing you to enter his great canal. We cast anchor by the row of offices along the quay, and many of us visited the shops for which Port Said is famous. Here you get African, Asiatic, Chinese and Japanese curios, silk shawls so fine that they will pass through a finger ring, ostrich feathers, silver ,spangled scarves, and excellent Egyptian cigarettes, at about a third of their cost in Europe. Port Said is indeed the clean-house of East and West ; their races and their commerce converge here, at the entrance to this wonderful canal.

All the next day we were steaming down it. On one side stretched the fawn coloured Arabian sands, on the other, the flat Egyptian marshes bounded by low hills. Such vegeta- tion as there was grew on the Egyptian side

div.head: CEYLON.
div.p: CEYLON.
Ceylon has a magic all its own. Ask whomsoever you will, who has been there, and they will agree. Though we only spent one day in Colombo, the enchantment fell at once upon us. It was of coursa hot,

div.head: ADEN.
div.p: ADEN.

and consisted of palms and other trees, and often great tufts of pampas grass. We saw our first camels here, and Arabs with long robes flapping in the chilly morning wind; for they are at work refacing part of the crumbling banks, and also dredging the bottom so that in future two large vessels may pass each other without one of them having to moor itself to the bank. The lights of Suez looked very pretty, glimmering across their lake. Next morning found us pounding down the Red Sea, which happens, by the .way,to be remarkably blue. Those of us who rose early, by whichsj mean six o'clock, saw Mount Sinai, hazy as a dream beyond the shimmering Arabian sands. There was now a great change in the temperature. Passengers produced summer frocks and flannels, and the officers and stewards appeared in white duck. This was partly due no doubt to that dreaded thing, a "following wind." The wind, that is to say, was travelling about the same rate as the steamer, and in the same direction. We could not get a cool breath, and were glad to turn on electric fans in our cabins, and put wind-scoops out of the port-holes. These are tin funnels, split in two, which project and gather in what air the vessel's speed creates.
Aden was our next port of call. • • "Old Aden like a barrack stove That's not been lit for years and years,"

as Kipling's soldier says. Contrary to expectations, our first sense was admiration at sight of the high jagged hills behind the town. The silhouette is splendid,but there isn't a single touch of green anywhere except in the Governor's garden. We landed, and were much amused to see the Somalis,

though we were in the early days of Decem- ber; but there is much tree shade in the wide streets. We each sat in a 'rickshaw,' and were run round the sights for a couple of hours, by the active, good-humoured Cingalee in the shafts. Great heavy-scented flowers trailed over fences and porches ; here and there the scarlet goldmore tree, ancia- leaved, spread branches of blood-red blossoms against the blue sky. The roads were covered with a soft crim§on dust, which flew up under the runners' feet, and acted much like rouge on our faces. I remarked to Miss Benson what a .plendid colour the sun had given her.. She returned the remark, and we were proportionately disappointed when we found that it washed off!

Seven miles from Colombo, the house of a former Governor of Ceylon stands on a little green promontory called Mount Lavinia. We drove out here for lunch, passing through palm and cocoa-nut groves all the way. The natives are very dark-skinned, and a con- tented, lazy:lot. The land so flows with milk and honey—unlike its great neighbour India—that the minimum of labour suffices for their wants, and taxes are very light, though the Government draws a relatively enormous revenue from the Island. Monnt Lavinia is still more dreamlike than Coluthbo. The little bay is lined with sands of dazzling gold, and the turquoise sea breaks creaming up the sands in smooth, slow progression. One or two of the cele- brated catamarans came sailing homewards before the warm breezes as we watched, and were beached quickly and beautifully. They are extremely narrow boats, being hollowed out of a single trunk with a log attached to one side at a distance of about two feet, to

act as ballast, I suppose: Anyway it steadies them wonderfully, and they carry a large sail. We heard a most curious fact about a catamaran which had recently foundered in a gale outside the bay. When the black-skinned crew were washed ashore, they were found to have turned chalk-white? and this is the effect of drowning on all dark-skinned people, as we later had occasion to see for ourselves. The heat was terrific from two till three o'clock, and we lay gasping in lounge chairs in the wide verandah of the hotel. Lovely Cingalese lace is hawked about, at absurdly low prices according to our ideas of work. But in'that happy, lazy land, where all strenuous endeavour and fighting for ideas would soon go to sleep, time is of no value; and the wife must spend days and days in making a lace collarette Which the husband, after the inevitable bargaining, will sell for two rupees (2s. 8c1.) We saw a quaint Bhuddist temple in the thick palm grove behind the hotel ; its walls were covered with frescoes representing scenes in the life of Gavtama, who became the Bhudda. As is probably well-known, although Bhuddism has nearly died out of India proper, it flourishes in Ceylon and Burma, and of course has an immense hold in China and Japan. We dined with friends at the Galle-face Hotel, reputed to be the best in all India, and admired the. myriad twinkling lights of the harbour as our tug streamed across it to rejoin the Syria, at the end of this magical day. Next morning we were running parallel with the southern and eastern coasts of Ceylon,at a distance of eight ' or ten miles. All day we watched the lovely shapes of the hills growing and fading, Adam's Peak towering sharply above the reNt ; whilst the warm sweet-scented air literally breathed spices over the waters, and peaceful red-roofed Point de galle crept into view in its snug bend of the shore, and then was slowly hidden. No wonder people rave over the beauties of Ceylon. They tell one that up in the hills it much resembles Scotland. A lady who lives on a plantation about 6,000 ft. up, said that for nine months of the year they had log fires in the evening. The few days which we took to reach Calcutta were amongst the least pleasant of the voyage. The Bay of Bengal remains to Tie as an impression of blistering • salt wind, an aching glare off the shimmering sea; and a terrific smell of " ghi " or melted butter, at stated times from the fo'castle, where the Lascars cooked it, and from which there was no escape since the wind was dead ahead and swept it down both sides of the deck, so that we took our evening promenade with hand- kerchiefs to our noses.

The Hoogli somewhat resembled the flat banks of the Mersey beyond Runcorn, except that it was far wider, and that now and then palms dotted the shores. Otherwise, ht a distance, Indian trees look much like English ones. We lay in Garden Reach some hours, waiting on the sluggish yellow tide. Every- one breathed more freely when the terrible shifting quicksand, called James and Mary from the name of a vessel lost there, was passed.

div.head: IN CALCUTTA.
div.p: IN CALCUTTA.

On the Wednesday morning we were achored by the great white buildings of Calcutta, where Miss Benson's brother, cousin and fiancé met her. The wedding took place next afternoon in the Cathedral, which is about the size of Warrington Parish Church, and is painted pale green for the sake of coolness. Sometimes, I believe, when the big liners come in, the Cathedral is kept hard at it for several days! I have nothing but the best recollections of Calcutta; partly because it was one's first Indian town, and the great, handsome white buildings impressed one; more because Miss Benson's happy wedding with Mr. Venters took place here; and most because kind friends put me up for a week and showed me all the sights and gaieties of the capital—and it was here that Sam, jewel amongst `bearers,' entered_ my service for close on three months.

To take things in order: Calcutta,of course, is an enormous and busy city, and about the only one where the slums are really bad in the native quarter. Against this one must set the palatial houses of the Europeans and rich Hindus. The gardens of these houses are often lovely; great scarlet poinsettias grew in shrubs round the drive of the house where I was staying. Mauve bougainvillia climbed everywhere, and tall trees threw a grateful shade on the garden. The tempera- ture was delightful, especially in the early morning, when the air was crisp and spark- ling beyond anything we know in England, and the pale blue sky. a joy to look at. Decem- ber and January are the season in Calcutta, and the Europeans put in a strenuous six weeks of gaiety and exercise. There are golf links out at Tollygunge, three miles off, which would compare favourably with many English ones; another links is on the Maidan, the great sunburnt common said to be five miles round, of which Calcutta is so proud. Here is the racecourse, ending in handsome stands and a beautiful little paddock and lawn, shaded by wide-spreading trees. The Zoo is another glory of Calcutta. It is laid. out in what was once, I believe, the garden of Warren Hastings; and the winding paths and sheets of water, and great blossoming trees make a lovely setting. The Botanical gardens are world-renowned ; and so are the Bengal Lancers, who form the Viceroy's body-guard, and are all men of great stature, wearing scarlet tunics, and deep-blue striped turbans. 'To see them charge down with wild yells at a tent- pegging competition is a sight not to be forgotten.

div.head: AN IDEAL SERVANT.
div.p: AN IDEAL SERVANT.

Sam, whose real name is Murray Venketa- swami, is, I should judge, considerably over sixty years of age. He is a Madrassee and a Bhuddist, which gets over much of the caste difficulty: and I shall never wish to havp a better travelling servant, nor cease to be grateful to the friends who procured him for me. He folded skirts and packed like an angel, polished one's shoes, brought one's tea to the train window, knew hotels, gave good advice about native dealers, and had. a fine sense of humour behind a grave and quiet manner. Above all, he was honest, which many hired bearers .are not; I never once found anything suspicious in his items, and he was genuinely devoted to one's interests. When Sam was introduced to me I was examining a small pistol, which had beeh given as a Christmas present, because thiev- ing was rather prevalent on the railways. I was trying the sight on the door, and as Sam came round the corner, he met the muzzle pointed full at him. In an instant he had melted away like the driven snow; but I think his sense of humour was at work when he reappeared. With this trusty servitor I quitted my kind friends in Calcutta two nights before Christmas. (To be Continued).
