div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, JULY 10Tir, 1909.
We are in the midst of A DIRECT what it is usual to call CHALLENGE. a." miniature general

election." There will be four contests in progress at one time. One of these is occasioned by death ; the other three are a consequence of Ministerial rearrangements. The Government, that is to say, has deliberately brought about three of the elections that are now, or will shortl y be in progress. This fact we put forward as an amply sufficient answer to those small- minded critics of the Birthday Honours, list who said that Mr. ASQUITH had not dared to make any Peers from members of the House of Commons because the Government is afraid of the opinion of the constituencies. We go much' beyond this. The vacancy in the High Peak Division of Derbyshire has been deliberately created for the purpose of ascertaining what a doubtful constituency thinks about the Budget. The Government has not selected a strong position, but a weak one. The case is much like that of the Frenchmen at the Battle of Fontenoy, who are represented as saying, " Please, gentle- men, you are first."

The authors of the Budget have given the Opposition a great chance. Let us see what they make of it. Even the most excited of Conservative party men will, we suppose, be capable of seeing some nobleness in a chal- lenge issued• under such conditions. The High Peak Division of Derbyshire was until recently a Conservative division. It was won by no very large majority. It is pervaded by the influence of the DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE. The enemy, sb to speak, has every possible local and accidental advantage. The creation of this particular vacancy for no particular reaton arising out of the eminence of the member who has been taken into the Ministry is, therefore, an invitation to a clean, straightforward, resolute fight on the

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, July 10, 1909.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, July 10, 1909.

great question of the Moment. An midistinguished constituency is selected for the battleground tbecause the chances are so nearly even.. What is being looked for is a genuine indication of popular opinion on the Budget‘

In Mid-Derbyshire the result of the con- test which is now in progress cannot be con- sidered doubtful. The Liberal majority is very large, and the Conservative candidate is obviously very ignorant of politics. One of his arguments is that the Government is afraid of legislation, and that it has there- fore put its Proposals into a Finance3Bill. What he supposes a Finance Bill to be remains unexplained. The Government has obviously taken the view that success in such a constituency as this could not be taken as a decisive indication of average opinions on its policy. It has sought the opinion of what may be called the con- stituency next door. There the seat was not long ago won from its opponents; the Liberal majority cannot be palled large; and there is a Conservative candidate of great wealth and extensive generosity. The popular opinion of the Budget is thus to be ascertained on fair terms.

May we point out in connection with this chivalrous arrangement that the Liberal party has never within living 'memory been shy of taking the public verdict on its pro- posals and achievements? Mr. GLIWSTONE faced the defeat of 1874 because a few bye- elections had gone against him, and despite the fact that the last of those bye-elections had gone in his favour. He had no desire to remain in power when once he felt that public opinion was going against him. .It was the same at a later date, when Home Rule became the burning question of the day, and it was the same again iri 1895, when Lord ROSEBERY'S Government chose to resign on a vote in committee which involved no question of resignation, and was brought about by one of the most contemptible pieces of trickery in the history of Parliament. We have no hesitation in making the broad statement that no Liberal Government in these days wishes to remain in office when in the absolute sense it is no longer in power.

We will not drive the lesson home by describing what should be in every man's memory. We mean, of course, Mr. BALFOUR'S retention of office long and long after he and everybody knew that an appeal to the country must mean such a debacle as that which ultimately took place. The question now in a sense to be decided by the bye-elections is one of tremendous con- sequence, to say nothing of what is falsely described as Tariff " reform." Does the country now hunger for• such•. another Go,vernment as that of Mr. BALFO.UR ? This question is particularly addressed for the moment to the High Peak Division of Derbyshire.

Th e Royal visitors THE RAPID have been and gone,and ROYAL VISIT. Warrington once more • wears its normal aspect after a few days of elaborate preparation and several weeks of eager anticipation. It , is an unhappy circumstance, but truth com- pels us to say that the Royal visit was not all that it might .have been. No blame attaches to the weather which, ever freakish, damped the ardour and the decorations of the townspeople in the early part of the day, only to smile sunnily on the scene at the moment the King and Queen and Princess Victoria were passing through the town. On this score there can be no ground for complaint, but the fact remains that the prevailing feeling in the breasts of Warring- ton's loyal inhabitants is one of sore dis- appointment. The Royal visit was all too hurried and brief. That is the trouble. Their Majesties passed through the town in a closed motor car at a speed which may have been slow for such high-powered vehicles, but which, from the point of view of the onlooker, was too rapid to afford more than a fleeting glimpse of Royalty. We may safely and sadly state that not much more than half the asseinbled thousands lining the route saw the King at all. Even during.the stoppage at the Town Hall little was seen of their Majesties, so short was, the visit, and almost before one' could realise that the ruler of the realm ha,d indeed visited 'Warrington on July 6th 1909, the Royal party were speeding onward over the road to Knowsley, paced by that energetic nobleman the Earl of Derby. Some- thing more, we think, Warrington had a right to expect, but it ill-becomes us to intrude with grumblings upon that" divinity which doth hedge a King." Our loyalty remains unshaken. We can only wish, deep down in our heart's, that the exigencies of a busy round of duties had not conspired to prevent Warrington from obtaining such a view of Royalty as would have left a glowing and indelible irnpressiori upon the minds of all, from the youngest and lowliest to the eldest and highest of a loyal community.
The question of A GIILI3ERTIAN seniority in the War- SiTuATioN. rington- _Town Council

approaches that humor- ous phase which it has become the custom to describe as Gilbertiau. On Tuesday evening next Councillor Wilkinson will Propose the rescinding of Standing Order 52, which determines seniority and precedence by the length of each member's service, and the sub- stitution of a standing order necessitating the service to be continuous and uninter- rupted. The amusing featur.e is this. Eleven years ago Councillor Henry. Roberts was elected an Alderman by virtue of just such a standing order in preference to Coun- cillor William Pierpoint, who had a break of three years in his tenure of office and thus lost the previous twelve years in the reckon- ing of seniority. Five years later this standing order waS rescinded and the present one substituted—the fairest proceth4e in our opinion. Now Mr. Roberts is once more a member of the Council, and according to the existing Standing Order he is entitled to count all his past service for seniority and claim the first Aldennanic vacancy, notwithstanding a break of nearly seven years In his tenure. Could the whirli- gig of time have brought about a more curious and amusing situation ? Naturally enough, Councillor Wilkinson finds fault with the present Standing Order, which bids fair to relegate him to a position junior to the new representative for, White- cross Ward. Mr. Roberts is in the odd situation of having been elected alderman by virtue of the first rule, sa_nd being entitled to re-election under the second ! What will the Council do?

The Prime Ministers MR. ASQUITH AT survey of the political SOUTHPORT. situation, at the • Annual Conference of the National Liberal Federation, was, it is hardly necessary to say, masterly and penetrating.* But it was inevitably to the Budget that he directed the larger part of observations, and 'of the Budget that his audience was chiefly thinking. There could not have been a more fair exposition of the scope and general effect of the so-called land-taxes; but because Mr. Asqnith refrained from entering into the technical details which are engaging the attention of the House of Commons at the present moment, Mr. Balfour afterwards essayed to convict the Prime Minister of a view of the taxes inconsistent with the line which the Government is following in its conduct of the Finance Bill. We may leave the pretended inconsistency on one side side for a little—it all turned upon a juggle with words-i-in order to consider Mr. Asquith's handling of the objections brought forward to the principles involved in the increment duties and the tax upon undeveloped land. Is it unfair or impolitic that the State should take its share in the increas_e in the value of land created by the expansion of popula- tion and by commercial expenditure? The Opposition reply, it is unfair because there are other unearned increments which you do not propose to tax. When such instances do occur, they are insignificant in amount and different in character: it is absurd to compare the sudden growth of a country doctor's practice because a colliery springs up in his district—a growth, too, upon which lie pays increased income-tax— with the unearned increment of a ground landlord. The objection of the Opposition is about as effective as if the only argument raised against a proposed poll-tax was that there were cases of headless men in shows who would be iiinfairly exempt. The objec- tion advanced against a small tax upon the real value of land which the owner holds back from use while its value grows by leaps and bounds is that it will tend to bring more land upon the market. What a calamity!
It is seven years NATIONAL SERVICE since Lord Roberts's IN ENGLAND. National Service

League emerged into the light of day. When it appeared most people declared that its conscriptionist propaganda would never - catch on in Eng- land at all, and the rest sagely predicted that a year or two 'would see it taken up by one of the great parties in the State. As usual, everybody was wrong; judging by the annual reports. the League has made steady but by no means extremely rapid progress. The member- ship has reached 30,000—something like the membership of the I.L.P. True, there are 50,000 " adherents " as well, but, as all the connection these need have with the League is to pay a penny and receive a -card, their value at a crisis is open to doubt. The gross income for 1908 was £lO,OOO, a fair sum, but no more than the militant Suffragettes took in the first quarter of the present year. The only election fought was that in Warwick- shire, where Captain Kincaid-Smith got plenty of credit for his honesty but remarkably few votes. Lo,rd Roberts still believes that each of his "grave warn- ings" will shock the nation out of its sleep (as the phrase goes), and the gallant old veteran optimistically expresses hope that his plan will triumph within five years. What may come ultimately we do not profess to say. The prophet's mantle is not for us. But, judging by the public's present temper, it will take very much more than five years to convert it to the principles of compulsory military service. The line taken by prominent civilians is an index. Of the well-known names in the list of guests at the League's annual dinner, practically all were names of retired Admirals and Generals. These be very excellent people all of them. But. they can be regarded neither as unbiassed nor as representative. Every man, to put it bluntly, tends to think that the expansion of his own trade would mean the salvation of the country.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Reano's band is a greai and irresistible attraction at tire popular Hippodrome this week, and crowded houses have been the rule nightly. Reano _claims to out-do Sousa, and as a conductor we think .he can substantiate his claim. The (treat American bandsmau had a style all his,own in the way of conducting; and we should hardly have thought that its extremes of bodily movement would.' have tempted anyone to emulate, let alone surpass it. Reano s. conducting is, • we should think, the " limit "in this class of business and it is certainly in its proper house on the music hail stage. He performs the most fearful and wonder- evolutionS with the baton, now and -then menacing the trombones with s mord-like gestures, anon literally drawing Music from the clarionets,and again list ning With a rapt expression to the bass.fiddle,his ear only a few inches from the strings. As the music gets wilder Reano is impelled to greater efforts • which culminate in him knocking over the conductor's music-stand, and falling exhausted into the front row of bandsmen as the curtain 'falls before the eyes of an almost Mesmerised audience. Then Rearrocomes to the front and gasps out words of thanks in response to the thunders of applause, his hand all the while pressed dramatically to an obviously 'palpitatiug heart. ,We ought to add that the band itself is remarkably profiCient and well-trained, and renders various selections with an effect hithertl undreamt Of. The finale of `-, NapOlean's Retreat from Moscow,". With red fire, bursting bombs in the wings, and , the blare of the trumpets must . be seen and ' heard to be realised. It is a musical cataclysm. Other turns in the bill attract their own share of I interest. Billy. Williams, humorous vocalist, Girtie Lewis,' male . impersonator, and Nellie Farrell with Irish songs, all indulge in solo efforts which bring a recall. The •Martelloni lady acrobats are great and the Granvillemccee I as Australian song illustrators. Altogether, the programme is a capital one, and a credit to the enterprise of the management. The other attroctions will be :—Carl Lynn, tke king of animal mimics ; Queenie West, comedienne and dander; Lona, in a charming musical act; Rose Cass, comedienne ; Ginnett's " Rejected Remounts " from the -Territorial Army ; • Leo Fields', the favourite comedian.

INVESTMENT PRACTICALLY • CONSIDERED. , From time to time we have referred to the valuable practical articles on investment subjects which have appeared in the " Financial Review of Reviews" from the pen of Mr. Henry Lowenfeld, the well-known writer on suchomatters. It has often:occurred to us that such articles, put into a more permanent form, would prove of exceptional value to the investor, and we are, there- fore, pleased to find, that the same idea has suggested itself to the publishers of the " Financial Reviev of Reviews," for they have just issued an excellent book of about 430 pages, containing a reprint of a number of the articles which have appeared in their publi- cation since it was established in 1933. The selection of the type of security best suited for the indvidual investor's requirements is indictted in the clur.se of this book, and the investor is aided in the seleztion of suitable localities for investment, which, of course, depends on wide discrimination between the respective worth of kindred securities which the investor may have in view, but the character of "Investment Practically Considered" is such that it sensibly assists the reader in arriving at an accurate 'conclusion. Not only to the investor is the book of value, but also to the student of political economy and social affairs, with which finance is, nowadays, intimately bound up.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., and Mrs. Cros- field attended the State Ball at Buckingham Palace last Friday night.

*-* * We hope the publication of a joke at the King's expense will not be considered lese majestie, or in bad taste. But when we heard "Edward the peace-maker" referred to as "Edward the pace-maker, the joke seemed to us too good to be lost in obscurity. * * *

We are glad to note that some progress has batn made with the scheme for the pro- vision of a verandah to shelter tramway passengers at Rylands-street corner, and particularly as the suggestion originated in these columns. Plans and _estimates have been got out, and it now rests with the owner of the Royal Court Hotel to meet the Corporation in a generous spirit. * *

Our readers will perhaps pardon us if we suggest that they are getting full value for their penny in this issue. Our illustrations of the Royal visit are on a scale never before attempted in local newspaper enterprise; we present the opening chapters of a new and exciting serial story 'entitled "Whose Hand " ? and the first instalment of a fasci- nating series of articles on travel by Miss Truda Crosfield. Tho " Examiner" will in future be made more and more a progressive people's paper ! * * * The Rector of Little Canfield,Eisex,refused recently to marry a couple between Rogation Sunday and Trinity Sunday, relying on an old canon of the Saxon period. It would do him good if his bishop inquired into his owri obedience to ancient canons. Does he observe the seven canonical hours of prayer? Does he have a corporas when he says mass, and a surnumblem under his alb? Yet further. Does ha take marriage fees? This last ques- tion is important, for by a canon of 1138 he is forbidden to do so under pain of excommuni- cation. * * * _ _ _

According to the minutes of the General Purposes Committee, the last meeting on the Warrington Bridge question broke up in some disorder, and business - was suspensed owing to the want of a quorum. The town had better wait till air-ships supersede such troublesome and brain-racking struc- tuKes as bridges. Judging by the rate of " progress " with the present scheme some such solution seems inevitable. Aviators will have solved their great problem long before the Bridges §ub-committee has found a glimmer of light. * *

As the Nationalists unanimously voted against the second reading of the Finance Bill, it is worthy of notice that Mr. John Redmond has declared himself unequivocally in favour of the so-called land taxes. Speak- ing at Arklow on Sunday, he reminded his hearers that the Budget placed no tax On agricultural land, and if any portion of the money wanted for Old Age Pensions had tb be met by taxation on any class in Ireland, the ground-landlords who,without expending a sixpence,had had the value of their property .increased by the growth and communal expenditure of towns, could most fairly and easily bear it. * *

In connection with the Royal visit, a curious coincidence much commented upon by the ladies assembled at the Town Hall, was the appearance of Mrs. A. H. Crosfield and Lady Greenall in the same colour scheme —tan, with black hats. The technical description of Mrs. Crosfield's toilette will doubtless be of interest to our lady readers. She wore a deep apricot gown of voile de soie over a shantung gown of same. The dress was trimmed with open-work embroidery which formed an opening down the left side allowing the shantung to be seen. A large picture hat with black ostrich feathers completed the toilette, * * *

The Rev. J.. A. L. Fellowes, rector of Bun- well, Norfolk, has fulminated against the Budget in his Parish Magazine, and has added the alarming threat that he shall reduce his Christmas gifts to the poor and all his subscriptions by one-half. He condemns the Budget root and branch, but his fury is chiefly directed against the Licensing Duties and the burdens on land. No doubt the rector is annoyed that his relatives are hard hit. One Fellowes owns half Huntingdon- shire, and another owns 4,000 acres in Norfolk. There are Fellowes and fellows— some not so bad as others, fortunately. This rector fellow, or Fellowes, seems rather a poor sport anyway. * * *

The King's visit to Lancashire is bringing joy and prosperity to the house-painters and a suggestion to the householders of London (says the " Westminster Gazette "). For the somewhat dismal towns and cities of the North-West of England have with one accord been painting the houses along the Royal route, and will present a uniformly clean face to the Royal eye. Whole streets will be all clean together, so far as the out- side of the platter is concerned. In London we are all at sixes and sevens, and when one house is painted it shouts derision at its neighbour, whose lease lets it go dirty for another year. Would it not be possible for all of us to paint our houses at the same time and once in a while pose as a White City? * * *

• Warrington was not the only place which had a real " flying" visit from the King and Queen. This is how the " Manchester Guardian" describes what happened at Barton :—" Unbelieving Barton.—We found the people of Barton looking rather woe- begone. They refused to believe that the King had gone by, for, as they said, were not Ship Canal officials in numbers still waiting to give him a greeting? This was a fact ; two steamers had been drawn close to the bridge, a bigger boat vivid with bunting, lay not far away, and there had been a hope that the King would stop at least a 'minute or two to be wished a good wish. But instead of any Royal halt the people of Barton saw only four motor carriages, with closed hoods, slip quickly past. One glimpse .of a scarlet tunic perhaps, or the nodding of a military cockade, and the party were gone. This would no doubt be only the advance guard, particularly as the King was not due for another twenty minutes, and the good people of Barton waited on. But that was all. The sight of a long string of every- day motors and cabs convinced them at last, and off they went."

div.head: Personal.
div.p: Personal.

We have heard that the Rev. Frank Vaughan has received a unanimous call .to an important London Church, but as yet he reserves hiSs decision. Chief Inspector Flood, of Warrington, was present at the Sanitary inspectors' Conference held at Glasgow' last week.

Dog Fancier's Success. We would call the attention of our readers to the announcement which appears in our advertising columns of an open-air musical festival, organized by the Warrington Workingmen's Infirmary Committee in aid of the funds of the institution, which will be held in Bank Park on Thursday, July 22nd. The combined male voice choirs - the Warrington Male Voice and the Apollo—with Crosfield's band, will render a choice selection of popular music. There will be no charge for admission but a collection will be made and all entering the park will be expected to contribute. A number of chairs will be provided, for which a small charge will be made. GOOD SECOND-HAND PIANOS, £5 55., £8 Bs., and £l2 12s. Others at higher prices. Fully guaranteed. Pianos tuned and repaited,—J. R. WOOD, 47. London rd., Stockton Heath. Advt. Parish Church Choir Excursion.

London was chosen as the .venue of the annual excursion organised by the adult members of the Warrington Parish Church choir. The party, number- ing 17, left the Central Station on Walking Day at 11.22. Travelling via Manchester, tht ough the Peak District by the Midland Railway, St. Pancras was reached at 3.47. After tea at Haneh'S Hotel in the Strand the party divided, some going to Kew Gardens and Richmond, the others remaining in town. Some visited Covent Garden Opera. On Saturday Morning, dividing into three sections, the party started sight- seeing, the places visited being Westminster Abbey, the Houses-of Parliament, Buckingham Palace (change of guard), Rotten Row, Albert Memorial, &c., return- in, to luncheon•at the Hotel at one p.m. After lunch the tower was visited by several, and then to St. Paul's for afternoon service, which was most impres- sive:, -Leaving St. Pancras at 5.35, the party journeyed. homwards, partaking of dinner en route. Warrington was, reached at 9.45, after one of the most successful excursions ever enjoyed. TILE KING'S VISIT.—FLAGS, STREAMERS, BUNT- " ING, etc, for sale or 11;re. Large stock.t-GARLAND, Bridge st., Warritigton.—Advt. Eimentary School Accommoiation, Holy Trinity Parish Magazine says:—" At a meet- ing of the school managers on Friday, June 25th, the following was sent to the Education Committee in reply to their request for the opinion of the managers on the Board of Education's proposal to reduce the accommodation of the existing elementary schools of the town by requirinc, ten square feet which up to now has been considered sufficient :—Dear reply to your letter of April 16th last, notifying the reduction, proposed by the Board of Education, in the town, and ,asking for the opinion of the managers thereon, I am instructed by our managers to point out that although Trinity Schools are not affected by the proposal, the cost of giving effect to it for the whole town must necessarily be very great; inasmuch as each scholar space lost by the reduction will require an outlay of about .tl5 a head when the accommoda- tion comes to be replaced.. As the reduction proposed will take about 2,009 scholar spaces the cost of replacement will be something like £30,000. The managers of Trinity Schools therefore, in considering the proposal, think the opportunity ought first of all to be given to the ratepayers of expressing an opinion as to whether or no the town can afford the luxury of providing the additional accommodation that the pro- posal requires.—l, am, yours faithfully, E. C. E. CARLETON. J. Moore Murray, Esq." •
TENNIS, CROQUET, AND GARDEN PURNITUE. J. S. GARLAND, Bridge se., WArrington.—Advt. A Furniture Removing Transactlon.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Deputy Judge Hyslop Maxwell,. John Lunt, contractor, sued James B..Bindloss, Park Avenue,- Ashton-on-Mersey, and formerly of Stockton. Heath, for /I 2s. 6d., for the removal of his furniture and work done. The defendant counter-claimed £3 for damage done to the furniture and to his house, alleged to have been caused through the negligence of the plaintiff's workmen.—Mr. Browne appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. Steel for the defendant.---The claim was admitted.-,--Mr. Steel stated that in_ September, 1938, the plaintiff contracted to remove the furniture to the defendant's new residence, and-in the course of removal various articles, including a piano, a sideboard, book case, table; wardrobe and three dining-room chairs were broken or otherwise damaged. Plaintiff had repaired the damage but the defendant complained that the work was inefficiently done.—After hearing evidence on both sides, the Deputy-Judge said he was not satisfied that defendant had made out his case, because during the corres- pondence he found that although the plaintiff was pressing for payment of the account for removal, defendant did not make any complaint as to damage until some Months aft,rwards. He gave judgment for the plaintiff on claim and counter-claim. • TRAVELLING TRUNKS, DRESS BASKETS, SITIT CASES, etc. Special lines at 175., 205., 225., and 20s.— GARLAND, Bridge st., Wercingt Dispute About an Assignment. -

At the Warrington Cott-I-ay Court on Thursday, before his Honour Deputy-Judge Hyslop-Maxwell, George Crump, 32, •Glazebrook-strcet, wholesale bedstead maker, brought an action. against William Hickman,. Lyme-street, furniture dealer, for the specific return of certain articles and tools of trade which belonged to him and which, he alleged, were -wrongfully detained by the defendant. In the alternative he claimed £35

the value of the articles /and £l5 damages for, detention.—Mr. Browne appeared for the plaintiff and .Mr. F. Cuthbert Smith, barrister (instructed by Mr. I'. S. Steel) for the defendant.--Plaintiff stated that in 19)5 the defendant took a bill of sale on certain stock in trade and on his household furniture and since that date Mr: , Hickman had made him considerable advances of money. On the • 24th April he executed a deed of assignment of the stock-in-trade at his works in Buttermnrket-street to Mr. Hickman for whom he worked for a fortnight from that date. Mr. Hickman however locked up the premises and refused to return him the tools. Plaintiff's contention was that there was an understanding that the toes were not to be ' included in the assihnment., Without calling upon the defence, his Honour held that the tools were iucluded in the assignment, ana gave judgment for defendant with costs.' -

THREE MONTHS FOR NEGLECT. SHOCKING CASE. At the Borouch Mice Court, on Tuesday, Thomas Woods, of 24, Gandy-streel,was charged nith neglecting his five children in a manner 1 kely to cause them unnecessary suffering and injury to health. Defendant pleaded "not guilt y."—Mr. A. Browne, who prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C., stated that the defendant was a journeyman butcher,but he resided with his wileat 42.4,Gandy-street. lie vould not nork, and went out early in the morning awl never came back until late at night. 'always under the influence of drink. During the past -three years he had never given his wife more than ss. per week. He had been named, ad left a good place .only for a trivial cause. He 9.01. s idle and drunken, and only for his brother the children vtould have fared even WOrSe. On the 29th of June, Lispector Cox went to the house and found the wife seriously ill. The younpst child was only five wreks old, and was very badly n.glected. The woman W 43 not • capable to looking after it. The other children have been grossly neglected and this man went out early in the morning well keowing the condition of his wife and children and never did anything to help them. The eldest child had an abcess on his neck and was being attended to at the hospital but the doctor's orde,s were not being carried out c wing to the illness of the m )ther and the neglect of the men. Itispector Cet advised th 3 mother to go to the Werkhouse Infirmary, who at first refused, but after eards assented and entered the Workhouse on Tourslay. and after being examined she nes fotind to be suffering from pneumonia, snd it was thought she was dying. however, he (Mr. Browne) had received a message that morning to say th it she was slight'y lietter.--Inspector Cox said that he visited the house and s tve the woman, woo appeared to him to be dying, and the b by was in a very neglected condition. The other children were fi:thy. The floor -of the house was also filthy, and %%as not fit for human beings to live in. The two children who nue going to -school appeared to be the best in health and cleanlin s. Tne man was capable of working. Witness sent for Dr. Peacock. He had also asked the defendant to obtain a relieving order, but he (witness) did not believe lie hal got one.—(Defendant: " Yes I did, sir.")—Steel Peers, a ledger at defendant's house, said he had kept the house going for over three years. He stayed there -solely for the sake of the man's wife. He paid 12s. per week for lodgings, and also paid the rent of the -house. Witness had to sleep on a made- ip bed in the kitchen.—Dr. Peacock said he visited the house and found the baby in an ema i 'Led condition. It only weighed 431bs. instead ot ?lbs. The four elder children were in a very dirty conlition. There was telly hat a loaf of bread and 60z3. of mlat In the house in the way of food. In his opinion the eendition of the childre I caused them unuecesstry suffering and injury to health.—Defendtnt was sentenced to three months bard labour.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday., July 10, '1909.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday., July 10, '1909.
OPEN-AIR POLITICS.
ANOTHER MEETING IN SUPPNT OF FREE TRADE.

The Pr ,gressive Lab yir LArtgi.e's pen-air campaign on t•elia f of Free Trade cominues w i ii unithate I enthut•iasin an';, notwithstanding the unfavour.tule weather, there was a good att.-nianca at the mt-e•ine held near Arpley Canons on \lc:inlay evening. Mr. J. Morton presided and the 13, iocipal speaker was Conn- &Dor Porter, of Manches-er. There were also on 'the Watt torn] :—Mr. C. E. Pon er, Mr. E. Wyt.ne Junes and Mr. Joseph Howes. The CHAIRMAN in a hr if aldress r.marked thtt the n-OrA hA listened to the speeches d•livered at the Tat HT Reform Leigue meeting, the less be saw in the Pr tEctionist tl:eory.

Councillor Poitetie. said they beard a great (Teal of talk about the Budget, and the challenge had been thrown down again and again to the Opposition. The suppotters of the Government said this was a Budget by which we wete raising £l-4.600,000 under Free Trade and they said to the other side: If If you don't Me this, what have you to offer in %change ?" He did not know whether at their big rnening o‘n Thursday the 'forks would say teey eete toing to tatse the m nay by taxing our food and manufactured articles, but up to now they had offered no alternative policy. One reason was that they were not all av reed on what they meant by tariff reform. They gave a different definition of it wherever they went, and Mr. Balfour's attitude had been a rid lie to ever, on-. As a simple illustration of what would happen under Protec- tion, the speaker pointed out that a manufacturer of boots, finding that rivals from America or Germany were selling boots perhaps a little cheaper than he was able to do, would go to the Governmept stud ask them to put a tax, sey, of 2s. per pair on foreign boots to keep them out. That sounded very nice and the manu- facturer for a little ehile would make a gee, I pile of money out of it, because he would immediately put up the price of his boots. When they heard wealthy manufacturers sticking up for tariff reform, they should remember that they were thinking about their own pockets. In En4land we used al.otat 100 million pairs of boots in a year and the tariff would mean that the price of those boots would go up 2s a pair. It was said that the men who made the I oots would get more wages, but when manufacturers made extra profits they did not immediately rue to their workmen and sey " You must hive half of tbis prefit." It very often had to be strewed out of them and he was afraid the wage earners would be a long time before they saw any rise in their wages he etuse of the tariff. Apart from the raising of the price of boots, the result would be that the men wh Made spades, pianos, or mousetraps, or the farmer who grew corn would go at (ince to the Government ant say "We want to keep our foreign rivals out" and the Government would have to put a duty on spaaea, mousetraps and pianos, awl, worst of all, they would have to put a duty on corn and wheat, which constituted the food of the great bulk of the people. Prices would therefore be raised all round ; and with their sovereign of wages they would not be aele to buy anythine like the same amount of goods they could now purchase. l'herefore if their wages went up to 21s. they would not get as much with them as they now received for XI. Men who were engaged as Postmen, policemen and clerks would not have any advance in wages and their expenditure would go up, FO that the effect would be equivalent to a reduc- tion of *agree Giving an instance of what could be achieved under Free 'rode conditions, • the speaker pointed out that at one time the Ameticans were sending in boots and beating our manu- facturers. In one case a manefacturer sent a man out to America to see how it was that Americans were able to beat us, and when he returned he said" Your machinery is out of date. Besides, you 'do not make your boots to.suit all classes-of customers " The English manufacturers began to " buck up," got hetrer machinery and made different sizes, with the result that they drove the American competition out of the country and between 190 L and MS there was a decrease per annum in the number of American b rots coming into this country of 1,380,0e0 prrs. Toe same thing happened in other industries. We bought o ir stuff in the cheapest market and if we found rivals tr 3 lug to outsell us we did not sit down and' whine or go to the government and beg and prey to them to shut out the foreign products. We set to work to fina out better machinery and improved methods of work in r. England was not a worn-out enuntry yet. The speak-'r quoted evidence given Lefore the Tariff Reform Com- mission to the effeat that the English motor car motet- facturer was gradually driving out the foreign motor car. Dealing with the cotton industry, the speaker asked how it was that we in England were able to beat the whole world in the neutral markets with our cotton yarn and cotton, cloth? For one thing we could build our cotton mills cheaper than any Protected country in the world. A milt of 100,000 spindles in the United States cost 50s. per spindle ; in Germany 375. and in F. tunes 345. Therefore, to erect such a mill in Pm United States they would have to expend £250.000, in Germany £185,000, and in ,Frauce .2175,00 e. In England the cost was 255. per spindle, or a total of £125,000. (Applause). The man with capital in England had therefore so much more left to pay better wages, and then he co iii se'l his yarn and cloth at a great advautage over the Protected countries. In the shipping industry we stood ye-eminent. England owned more thin half the ships that sailed over the waters of tbe globe. In 1907 there were 1,600,009 torts launched by Great Britain an.l 1,700,003 tons launched by the r-st of the world. iVe sold to the rest of the world last year abent 10.1 million pounds worth of ships. In 1860 the United States bad 21 million tans of shipping sailing under the American flag; in 1906 it had gone down to one million. In 1869 Gnat Britain had 4.1 million tons of shipping ; in 19,6 it had gone up to I I million tons. Why? Because we charged nothing on .the material :that came into this country to build our ships. Further, when the ships were bailt we could work them at 30 *or 40 per cent, less cost than the American ships, because the provisions and everything about the vessels, were so much cheaper with es. Ouly a year or two since the American Consul at Calcutta stated in an official report that so far as he knew, for, many years no ship wailing unier the Arneric m flag ea,l entered any Indira port and during that time mine,' thousands of British ships must h we entered. Mr. Chamberlain made a great show about our tin plate industry I eine, reined. The McKinley tariff imposed a dirty of 45 per cent on tin !Atte going into the United Stites. Th.re were only abotf 15,000 nen through- out the whole states employed in the tin plate industry but 11 the other hand there were about 2,000,000 employed in the an teatries that naed tin plate. The result of the e,riff was that tin plate went up 45 per cent in price arid the people who used it for canning salmon and lobster and fruit could not buy it. Their trade was almost ruined beciuse they had to agitate for years and years before they could get any relaxation of the tariff. It was stated at the end that it would have paid the United Sta' es better to have bought up all the tin plate woks and to have pensioned hand- somely all the 15,000 ram n than to put the tax on, because of the great loss to the other 2,000,000 of the community. What was the effect of the tariff in England? At first it lessened our exports of tin plate to the United States and some of our people s rffeted a bit, Wens in the case of the boot tradeetea manufacturers adopted better methods and foteel out new markets, and to-day the tin plate industry was more thriving than ever it was. 01.1 y last week he read of a new tin pinto works [ming built at C ,rdiff with a capital 0fi250,e00. Councillor Porter concluded by urging his Leareis to do their utmost to hand on the blessings of Free Trade to the future generatlons, for he believed that when- ever England abandoned Free Trade she would begin to tread the downward path and the glory, honour and sepremacy of the country would disippear. (Applause). Mr. C. E. PARKER confirmed what Counciller Porter had said with regard to the buot trade. The boots coming into this country from abroad never amounted to more than 2 per cent of our whole manufacture, yet for the sake of keeping out that 2 per cent., tariff reformers proposed to put a tax upon bouts. Owing to our importing Aneatican machinery arid ad rpting American method., our imports of b o:s hid been going down ste idily for the last six years. It was the same in every trade that the tariff reformers had wanted to protect. A few years ago a great many bicycles were comihg in from America. We copied the American methods, and improved upon there, and beat them in the bicycle trade. The same thing held good with regard to motors. Then again, we used to fear a lot from the joiners &tout the imported windows and doors coming in, mooly from Canada. We now made these and had been able to keep out tire foreign articles iii the right way—by beeting them on their merits. The tariff reformers' way was to foster a trade by coddling it and enabling the manufac- turers who were not tip to date to go on in the same way. He was often asked why he (lid not go in for tariff reform, as it was said it would I e a grend thing for him as a manufacturer of leather and he would make

a fortune if the 'trade were protected. What did Pro- tection mean in Germany, for instance? The tanner had been hit by a tax upon his raw material. The con- tention was—and it was a natural contention—that the farmer who grew oak in that country had a right to be protected, so they put a tax upon the tanning material coming into Geraiany. If the whole of the Waning materials coming into this country weritaxed in the same measure as they were in Germany the tanners would have to pay an extra £75,000 for them. If the hides coming into this country were taxed in the same way as those going in'o America, the amount they would have to pay extra for their hides would be £600,000. The leather tariff reformer said: "We won't tax the things that g) to tanning. We will only tax them after the leather has been male, and we can hand It on to the boot manufacturer." No doubt the leather men in Grmeny and America took that line, but the men who raised the hides in America—the cattle-growing people —said " We must have our share of the plunder, so if you protect the biota, clothing and everything which 'we es farm- rs have to buy, it is only fair that we as cattle raisers should have our share in the general taxa- tion." So they hal to put a tax on the hides in America. They were trying to take It off now, but they would have a difficulty, because the Western States which ra'scd the cattle had got their teeth into the biscuit, and they wero going to hold it. It was very doubtful indeed whether the manufacturing States would be able to get their hides du'y free. Continuing, Mr. Parker said they ceuld not treat Protection as applicable to one traee only. When a man narrowed his vision to his own triide and asked the question" Would it not be a good thing for my own trade, if I had a tax? "he cert&iily said " Yes." But if he got Protectipn for his Tart icular trade, every manufactarer and worker in the other industries would claim the same right, and will ea erything protected we should be not only no letter off but a great deal worse off than when we started on the foolhardy game. Protection was a I question which towhed the interests of the workers far more than those of the manufacturers. It. Was an it ural thing .for the manufsoturer, hoping that be would get a special tax upon his manufacture, to go in for Pro- tection, but when they took the great welfare of the abole of the people, undoubtedly their interest-was in bolding firmly to N'ree Trade. (Applause). Mr. JOSEPH How ES, in m 'sing a vote of thanks to the chairman and speakers, slid the "new taxers " were •idvertising a meet'ng in celebration of Mr. hamberlaufs birthday. The audience, boa ever, would not hear much about Mr. Chamberlain's birthday bat a great deal about the Budget. The meeting vtas the commencement of the Tory campaign in opposition to the Budget, bet instead of honesely stating tie fact, they pretended it was a meeting to celebrate Mr. Chamberlain's birthday. The Free Traders, however, were determined to be in a*, the celebration and the town would be posted with the following message from Mr. Chamberlain :—" If you are to give a prefereice tc the Colonies you must put a tax on food." That was the message Mr: Chan:lb.:A tin gave to the nation and the present was the pr iper time ti revive it Mr. Homes annouicil the irrantion of the Progressive Labour Le ague to hold two simultaneous dernonstratlons in support of the Budget, to be addressed by members of Parliament. Dealing with the imperial aspect of the fiscal question, Air. Howes said that if any arrangement were made with the Colonies, it must be two-sided. We already gave the Colonies open ports lust they gave us a well of tariffs. If there was ti be any re-arrangement, let them pull down their tariff walls and be equal aith us. Alluding to the taxation of land values, Mr. Howes said Southpoit, which was now a inkolifi3ent town, at one time consist-(l largely of sand hills. Now it was of immense value arid about two men had pocketed all the plunier. If the present Government's Budget. had bean in operation when they commenced toimild and beautify Southport, the increased incone alone would have paid all the rates and taxes of South- port. The lanfowners hid bade good innings and they ought not to grumble at paying a little now. When they talked about kaocking off taeir subscriptions to charities they st iod condemned by their own words, for it showed that their charity had not been charity at all. The members of the Labour League would defend the Budget in all its clams s. (Applause). Mr. E. WYNNE JONES sec indei and announeel that the B )rough Member would speak at one of their meet- ings at au early date. It the Tories defeated the Budget, their only nice native was Protection and work- ingmen must fight ag just th it to the last ditYn. Toe Liberals had prove] tithe hilt that they could raise the necessary revenue tinier a Free Trade system. (Applau-e). • The vote was heartily passed.

div.p: THE OXFORD CAPTAIN

At Lords in the beginning of this week Oxford and Cambridge met in their great annual encounter. It is an old theory that the 'Varsity captain who gets two noughts Vut wins the toss, is ,much more than worth his place in the side. Mr. C. S. Hurst, the Oxford captain, was lucky enough to win the toss on Monday, and in the photograph given above he shows his pleasure at the happy circum- stance.
Owing to play being interrupted by rain the match was drawn, Oxford having the advantage of the scores. Oxford, 207 and 191 for 8 (declared) ; Cambridge, 183 and 89 for 4.

Said to Relieve Rheumatism, and Anyone Can Prepare it.

Thousands of men and women who have felt the, sting and torture of this dread disease which is no respecter of age, person, sex, na ion or rank, will be interested to know, alit while for many years rheu- matism was considered an incur:elle dissese,now it is one of the eisiest afflictions of the human body to conquer. Me.iical science his proved that it is nit a disease in itself, but is a symptom cau3ed by inactive Isidneys. Rheumatism is uric acid in the blood and other waste products of the system, which should be filtered arid stran-d out in the forte of urine. The function of the kidneys is to &ft these poisons and alids out., and keep the blood clean and pure. The kidneys, howece-, are of sponge-like sub- stance, the holes or pores of which will sometimes, either from overwork, cold or exposure, become clogged and inactive, end failing in ,their function of eliminat- ing these poisr.ns fro:n the blood, they rem-iin in the veins, decompose, and settling ahout the joints and mu-cks cause the untold pain and suffering of rheu- matism, and backache, often producing complications of bladder and urinary disease, weaknes4, etc. The following simple prescription is said to relieve the worst cases of rheumatism, because of its direct action upoa the blood and kidneys, relieving. too the most severe forms of bladder and urinary troubles; Tincture Gentian Gimpound, one ounce; Syrup Rhubarb, one evince; Liquid Barkola Compound, one (mace; and Syrup of Ginger, five ounce. Mix by shak- ing well in a bottle, and take one teaspoonful after each meal, and one befo-e retiring for the night. The in.;redients c,n he had from any good chemist. and being purely vegetable, are entirely harmless, are safe t 3 use at any time.
RIISCORN MAN DROWNED IN PRESENCE OF HIS FATHER.

Capt lin Thomas Burrows, master of the flat Excelsior, whose home address is 52, Ca.wdor•street, fiuncoin, on Ttie.sd iy informed the polic3 at Brulis ale( Dock of the accidental drowning of his son, William Burrows, aged eighteen 3ears, one of the hands working the flat. The youth was fngaged at 7.10 a.m. in a small boat, from xhich he hid nude fast a line to the di edger, Tantalus, in order to haul the flat itA,3 the Ccburg Dock. On looking round to see how th 3 operati.,r, was proceeding, Captain Burrows missed his son from the boat. The young min could not swim. Grappling was at once commenced, and about eight o'clock the body was recovered aid remoi el to the Princes Dock Mortuary.

in full regalia, occupied a special stand in Church- street. A welcome break in the monotony of waiting for the Royal visitors was afforded by the appearance of the guard of honour of the 4th Battalion South Lancashire Regiment who marched through the streets headed by the band of the battalion and carrying one of the handsome colours presented by the King at Knowsley on Monday. They looked exceedingly smart in their scarlet uniforms, carried themselves in true soldierly style, and gained the warm applause of thousands of onlookers. The band from Orford Barracks also played martial airs on the route. As the time for the visit drew nearer, detachments of school children, in charge of their teachers, could be seen making their way in procession to the special places allotted to them. They were attired in Sunday best, looking spic and span, and most of them displayed a ribbon or favour of some description. The places where the children had to stand were barricaded, so that there was no risk of accident. The first youthful assembly to meet the gaze of those entering the Borough was drawn up near Bruche Bridge; and there were others at Howard Place and in Liverpool-road. The greeting "The School Children of Warrington wish Princess Victoria many happy returns of the day" was prominently displayed.

div.head: AT THE TOWN HALL.
div.p: AT THE TOWN HALL.

Brilliant indeed was the scene at the Town Hall where an assembly, truly representative of the munici- pality, had assembled to await the arrival of their Majesties. It must have been realized by all present how peculiarly favoured Warrington is in possess- ing, in the centre of the borough, a civic mansion standing in such picturesque grounds, for a more suitable setting for the event of the day could hardly be conceived. The greensward, thanks to the most careful preservation, was looking at its best, and the massive fountain sent forth cooling sprays. Several hundreds of invited guests were accommodated on two stands covered with red baize. The elite of the district were there, and the charming dresses of the ladies gave a rich colour to the scene which was one to be long remembered. The guard of honour of the 4th Battalion South Lancashire Regiment was drawn up on the lawn, the King's colour being in the fore- ground, and the battalion band discoursed sweet music. Several members of ti e Legion of Frontiers- men, in their scout-like uniforms, were present in the grounds. Below the balcony of the Town Hall was an interesting, unostentatious yet truly distinguished group. It consisted of thirteen military veterans— fine old men who have fought England's battles in the Crimea, India, Persia. and Turkey. Proudly they bore their medals on their breasts and with eagerness did they await the approach of their Sovereign for whose predecessor they once gladly hazarded their lives. THEIR MAJE.

Though the weather during the earlier part of the afternoon was unpromising, there was a welcome improvement as time wore on, and a few minutes before their Majesties were due to reach the borough the sun broke through and continued to shine brightly. It had just turned six o'clock when the elegant and powerful motor cars containing their Majesties, Princess Victoria and suite arrived at Bruche Bridge. There was great disappointment when it was seen that the cars were covered, for this meant that the pros- pects of obtaining a good view of the Royal visitors would be somewhat remote. A detachment of mounted police was in readiness, Lord Derby, who was in the first car, signalled to them to lead the way, and at a quick pace the procession passed on its way to the Town Hall. As before stated, only those spectators who were very near to the roadway were able to see their Majesties, and in consequence the cheering was not very pronounced—in fact many in the crowd did not conceal their sense of disappointment.

div.head: CEREMONIES AT THE TOWN HALL,
div.p: THE CEREMONIES AT THE TOWN HALL,

When the news that their Majesties had entered the Borough reached the Town Hal I, the Mayor (Alderman Forshaw), wearing his robes and chain of office, and attended by the mace and sword bearer, took up a position at the foot of the steps, and the Mayoress and the other ladies and gentlemen who were to be pre- sented also assembled in readiness for the ceremonies A cheer proclaimed the near approach of the pro- cession and a few moments later the mounted police were seen coming almost at a gallop up the East drive. The nine motor cars quickly followed and the whole of the occupants of the stands rose and extended an enthusiastic greeting to their Majesties who were in the second car. The order in which the cars arrived was as follows :

The Territorial Band played a verse .of the National Anthem and the guard of-honour saluted as the Royal car drew up before the green dais which had been placed below the balcony. The King, who was wearing the uniform of a field marshal, returned the salute and the Queli bowed graciously. • Tunnedi- ately the procession came to A standstill, Lord Derby left the first car and opened the door of the R yal conveyance. The Mayor then , advanced and was introduced by Lord Derby to His Majesty who shook hands and smiled. Next came the presentation of the loyal address on behalf of the inhabitants. Addressing the King the Mayor said : May I have your Majesty's permission to present to you on behalf of the inhabitants of this loyal and ancient borough this loyal address of welcome.

'His Majesty graciously signified his consent, where- upon the Mayor handed him a silver cylinder contai !l- ing the address which had been tastefully illuminat-d by students of the School of Art and read as follows :
To his Most Excellent Majesty King Edward VII.

May it please yicur Majesty, We, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal sub- jects, the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington, humbly desire to offer to your Majesty and to her Majesty Queen Alexandra a grateful and most cordial welcome to our ancient Borough on the occasion of the review by sour Majesty of the Territorial forces of the West and East Lancashire.
We desire to express our great gratification and appreciation of the high honour conferred upon the town and its inhabitants by your Majesty's gracious visit.

We avail ourselves of the privilege of offering to your Majesty our most earnest and loyal wishes that the lives of your Majesties may be long spared to reign over your loyal and devoted subjects in continued peace and happiness. . Given under our Corporate Seal, this sixth day of July, 1909.
Wm. J. FORSHAW, Mayor. J. LYON WHITTLE, Town Clerk

His Majesty then motioned to the Bight Hon. R. B. Haldane, the Minister in Attendance, who, resplendent in his Windsor uniform, had taken up a position on the dais, and received from him the following type- written reply, which His Majesty then handed to the yor

I am much gtatified to receive the loyal and dutiful address from the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the ancient borough of Warrington. In coming among you to-day to review the Territorial Forces of the cuunty, I am reminded that your town and district have witnessed in time past many conflicts between hostile forces, but I am confident that the patriotic spirit of my people is as strong as ever, and that no effort will be wanting to prepare for any risk, however remote. I trust that by God's blessing the warlike scenes of the past will not recur, and that you will be able to pursue without interruption the arts and pursuits of peace by which your town has become prosperous. You may be assured that I shall always take the

liveliest interest in your welfare. The Mayoress, Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall, the borough member (Mr. A. H. Crosfield) and Mrs. Crosfield were then successively presented to His Majesty, the ladies making: a deep curtsey and the gentlemen bowing. His Majesty received them with great geniality and cordially shook hands with them. Meanwhile, at the other side of the Royal car another pleasing little ceremony was enacted, Miss Edith Forshaw presenting a bouquet of Lancaster roses and ferns to her Majesty Queen Alexandra, and Miss Bessie Forshaw handing a bouquet of Mahnaison carnations to Princess Victoria. The gifts were smilingly acknowledged. The crowning touch of the proceedings was the present tion of a birthday gift to Princess Victoria. The Alayor said : "May I have the permission of your Royal Highness Princess Victoria to present to you this birthday gift from our loyal town," and thereupon handed to the Princess a diamond necklace The present evidently afforded her Royal Highness much pleasure and she received it with a few words of thanks.

Three minutes had sufficed for the whole function which was now at an . end. The door of the Royal motor was closed; the other distinguished gentlemen in attendance took their places in their respective c,.rs, the band again played the National Anthem, and the procession swept on its way to Knowsley while the assembly joined in a rousing cheer. His Majesty repeatedly saluted and the Queen bowed ni response. The historic event was over and the stands were quickly deserted. With such rapidity had the succession of ceremonies been performed, that before the onlookers had had time to realize that His Majesty had really arrived, he was ready to resume his progress to Knowsley. All along the route to Sankey 13ridges there were cheering multitudes and the [loyal visitors must have been gratified at the demonstrations of loyalty which heralded them on every hand. Promptly to scheduled time the procession left the borough, the Territorials, soldiers and mounted police quickly returned to their quarters, an the roadway again became thron ed with people inspecting the decorations.

div.head: FIREWORKS DISPLAY
div.p: FIREWORKS DISPLAY

The day's rejoicings wound up with a fireworks display in Victoria Park, arranged by Messrs. J. M. (litenhalgh and Co., in conjunction with Me-srs. J. Pain and Son (pyrotechnists to the King.) Many thousands of spectators attended, all the school children having free admission. It was rather unfortunate that the opening of the programnte was delayed considerably beyond the advertised time as many of the children were thoroughly tired out after the exertions of the day. The display was really magnificent and included a great variety of rockets, eh borate set pictures of the King and Queen, beautiful fairy fountains, illuminated moving figures of an elephant and a monkey-up-a-stick which affo.ded great delight to the youngsters, and a thrillin repre- sentation of a naval battle, ending with the blowing up of a warship. .The Cheshire Lines band played pleasing selections.

div.head: ILLUMINATED CAR
div.p: THE ILLUMINATED CAR

In honour of the Royal visit °tie of the tramcars was gorgeously illuminated and decorated, the work reflecting much credit upon Mr. J. Telfer, tramways manager, and the maintenance staff who had had it in hand. There were no fewer than 600 lamps stained in various colours and the effect was brilliant in the extreme. On each side of tha car appeared large crowns illuminated with sixty lamps each, and the Royal Monogram " E.R." and the Borough Arms were also introduced. Gay streamers and artificial roses and ,leaves put a charming finishing touch to the scene. The car was run on all routes on Monday and Tuesday nights and gave much pleasure to the public.

div.head: ILLUMINATIONS,
div.p: ILLUMINATIONS,

The brilliant illuminations at the Electricity Works attracted much admiration. The Royal monogram was displayed in letters 9 feet high awl a powerful electric search light cast its gleams over the town.

div.head: TRAMWAY RECEIPTS,
div.p: TRAMWAY RECEIPTS,

The abnormal traffic on the electric car service during the day swelled the receipts very considerably. The total takings on Tuesday amounted to :E147, which is .£4O more than the sum received on ~ny day since the opening of the tramways.

div.head: AMBULANCE ARRANGEMENTS,
div.p: AMBULANCE ARRANGEMENTS,

Warrington is fortunate in having a str ag ambulance corps, and the members willingly volunteered their services on the day of the Royal visit. The arrangements were admirably carried out by the officers under the direction of Captain Waring, the chief superintendent. Ambulance stations were formed at the following places, and consisted of four men and one nursing sister :—Bruche Bridge, Cemetery, St. Elphin's Park, National Schools, Howard-place, Scotland-road, Market-gate, Bold-street, Springfield-street, Crostield-street, Green-street, St. Luke's Church and Black Horse. Officers and sergeants patrolled between the stations. Each station was supplied with a stretcher, smelling bottles, bandages, &c. There was also a wheel litter at each of the following stations :—Rylands Bros., the Arch, Bank-street and Crosfield's. Headquarters division supplied all stations from Bruche Bridge to Spring- fiel&street, and Crosfield's division all stations from

There were also present :—Alderman Burton and Councillors Ashcroft, Birtles, Broadhurst, Craik, Dickenson, Dr. Joseph, Lasbford, Locker, Lord, Pemberton Rogers, Sankey, Skelland, Steel, J. Fulton- Smith, O'Toole, Wilkinson, Wilson, and H. Roberts. with the Town Clerk, Deputy Town Clerk, and the Director of Education. The Council made an order for the regulations of traffic, closing the whole of the route of the Royal procession at ,fp.m. and Buttermarkst- street to pedestrians at 4.45, and authorising the barricading of certain streets and passages. The CHAIRMAN said they bad now to consider an estimate of the expenditure in regard to the King's visit. At a meeting of the Finance and Executive Committee, it was decided to request the Town Council to vote the sum of £1,200 by way of salary to the Mayor to cover the expense. At a meeting of the committed that evening, it had been explained that, through the Mayor, the Council were practically Councillor PEMBERToN interrupting) : Will it be competent to move that the Council go into committee? Councillor LOCKER: I second. Councillor WILSON: I move an amendment. The CHAIRMAN : You can simply vote against the motion.

discussion on the question in the presence of the Press it was bound to go before the public and he for one objected most decidedly to that course being adopted. Councillor LOCKER: That was my reason for seconding the motion. I am afraid that something might be said we should not like to go out. The Council then divided, and the resolution to go into committee was passed by It votes to four. The public and Press then retired.

After close upon an hour's discussion in private, the Press were admitted and the Council unanimously passed the following resolution :—" That a sum not exceeding £1,200 be voted to the Mayor as remuneration for his services, and that the Finance and Estate Com- mittee be requested to drsw a cheque in favour of the Mayor for that amount." The CHAIRMAN then moved the following resolution: —" That a suitable present be made to Princess Victoria, in commemoration of her birthday, and that the follow- ing committee be appointed to arrange for it :—Coun- cillors Pemberton, Wilkinson, Sankey, H. Roberts and Locker."
Councillor LOCKER: I wish to withdraw from the committee.
The CHAIRMAN: You are too late. Councillor LORD seconded the resolution which was passed unanimously. LOCAL TERRITORIALS AT THE KNOWS LEY REVIEW.
The King, who was accompanied by the Queen and Princess Victoria, reviewed on . Monday in Knowsley

Park the West Lancashire Territorcal Division and other troops to the number of about 16,000. Probably 50,000 people attended the review, which included a presentation and consecration of colours. It was a public holiday in Liverpool, and many more people would have been in the park, but the road between that city and Knowsley became blocked with tramcars, motor-'buses and cabs, and other vehicles, so that while the review was ending hundreds were endeavout- ing to find a way to the ground. The 4th Battalion PrinJe of Wales's Volunteers (South Lancashire Regiment) was strongly represented at the review and the smart appearance of the men called for favourable comment. The battalion fell in at the Drill Hall at Warrington at 10.30 under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel J. D. Fairclough, the other officers present being Majors B. Eairclough and Appleton, Captains Croafleld, Smith, Cary, Rot ens, Williamson, Avery, Layton and Owen, Lieutenants F. R. The Rev. W. Bracecanip (chaplain) and Sergeant-Major Ingram were also present. The strength of the battalion at Knowsley, including officers, was as follows :—Wairington : 35 sergeants and 468 rank and file. Newton : Four officers, ten sergeants and 188 rank and file.

The local arrangements were complete in every detail and it is impossible to speak too highly of the work of the various committees and officials who dis- charged their exacting duties with zeal and tact. Special m,ntion must be made of the rown Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon k'k hittle) and his staff, upon whom the bulk of the -work,including a great mass of correspondence, devolved. It was cheerfully and efficiently done, no effort being spared to ensure that everythiug should pass off without a hitch. The Borough Surveyor (Mr. T. Longdin) did va uable service in the preparation of the route, under the direction of Lord Derby, who has acted on behalf of His Majesty. The Mayor, of course, threw himself heart and soul into the. arrangements and he was well baCked. up by the Reception Committee. As already stated the police were under the direction of Chief Constable (Mr. M. Nicholls) fulfilled their imnor,ant duties with conspicuous credit and success.

div.head: PRESENTED TO THE KING.
div.p: PRESENTED TO THE KING.

During tLe proceedings at Knosisley Colonel J. D. Faircluugti V 1 as presented to the King with other nfficers. Alderman Smethurst, as the lay representative of Warrington on the division, also had the honour of being presented. Amongst the Warringtonians present at the review were the Mayor and Ma3oress of arrington, Alderman and Mrs. Smethurst, Colonel and Mrs. Edelsten, Mrs. Reginald Smith, Miss Ridgeay (Daresbury), and Mrs. Denaham (Orford).

div.head: RECEPHON AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: RECEPHON AT WARRINGTON.

The return of the battalion to Warrington was awaited by a great concourse of people and when the men reached "the good old town" at .o.tiO they marched through the principal streets, beaded by the band. The uevil3-presented colours were proudly displa)ed and their apporrauce was the signal for a great outburst of enthusiasm. At the Town Hall there was a civic receptii n, the Territorials being drawn up on the lawn. Amongst those vs Ito assembled on the Town Hall steps were :—The Mayor, Mr. and Mrs. Robert Pierpoint, Alderman Smethurst, Bennett and Tinnion, Councillors Wilkinson, Steel, Fulton- Smith, Brcadburst and Wilson, Captain and Mn. A. F. G. Potter, and the Town Clerk abd the Deputy To an Clerk. The MAYOR addressed the men as follows: As the Mayor of this loyal and ancient town I vielcorue 3ou tack from Knowsley. I was exceedingly pleased to see you there to-day, because I thought you were the smartest men in the whole of the South-West Lanca- shire Division. (Applause.) I was also exceedingly pleased to find that you carried your colours with you and that your hand played that good old tune, "Long live the King." I hope 3ou will be as smart to-morrow as you have been to-day, when you will be reviewed here by the greatest monarch upon the face of the earth I wish you good luck " and " God-speed." (Applause.) Hearty cheers for the Territorials arid for the Mayor and Mayoress concluded a ceremony which, while very brief, will rank as a notable one in the history of the town and of the battalion. SUPPLY COLUMN.

The Warrington company of the Territorial and Supply Column also participated in the great review at Knowsley. They paraded 80 strong at the Drill Hall at eleven o'clock under the command of Captain J. 'l'. Piekton, the other officers on parade being Captain R. M. Roberts, Second-Lieutenants H. Fairclough, and J. S. Richardson, and Staff-Sergeant-Major Bullen. They proceeded by special train to Rainhill with two fully- equipped waggons. After leaving the train they pro- ceeded by road to Knowsley, where they joined the other companies of the column from Southport and Liverpool. After the review, the mounted section returned to Warrington by road, which was reached by nine o'clock, the remainder of the company arriving by special train at 9.15.

At the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesd.y, Mt', E. L. Bent, as chair- man of the Padgate Cottage Homes Committee, reported that the King did everything the Committee asked him to do in slowing down at Woolston. The children had a grand view of his Majesty, and he (the speaker) was sorry that more Warrington people were not up the Manchester-road, for it proved to be about the best position it was possible to get. He had heard a few comments from the townspeople that they were disgusted with the rapidity of the King's progress through the borough, as they scarcely saw him. At Woolston, however, they had a beautiful view, and the cars went past very slowly. He moved that a vote of thanks be passed to Mr. Joseph Houghton, who kindly placed a field at their disposal, and to Lo d lltrby for arranging for the cars to slow down.

A Historical Survey.

Unless there be in some odd corner a nonagenarian whose memory can reach back to George IV. there is no inhabitatit who retnemberS a royal visit to War- rington. Since the carriage of the coarse, unpopular Regent rolled from the George Inn (henceforward so-called in his honour) no monarch. so far as is known, had driven through the streets of Warrington until the advent of the King on Tuesday last. Royal visits to Warrington have indeed been few and long between Counting the last only four are on record during the past two centuries, and to count a fifth we go back another full century to the famous visit of Henry VII. in 1495.
