PARISH COUNCIL MSETING.—A special Parish Council meeting was held in the new Council schools, Stocks. lane, on Monday evening, there being present : —Dr. Murray, J.P. (in the chair),Mr.Withinshaw, Mr. Wood- ward and the Clerk (Mr. E. Foster.)—The Chairman explained that the meeting had been called with refer- ence to the sewer, as the present one had proved inade- qtrite to take away the flushes fro n the new schools w c.—Mr. Woodward said he did not think the meeting should proceed, as he believed this was a matter of spending about kso.—Mr. Withinshaw than proposed:—" That this Council recommend the Rural District Council to lay a sewer of 9in. pipes which would serve in years to corne.—Mr. Woodward: I think we ought to have a full meeting.— The Chairman said that meoibera of the Council had received due notice of the meeting.—Mr. Woodward : I don't think that they know that it is so serious as it is:—The Chairmen: I don't think I ought to second Mr. Withinshaw's motion, but as there Is no one else here I have no alternative but to second it.—The proposition was carried.—Mr. Woodward did not vote. —The date of the next meeting was thEn fixed for July 19th.

THE RECENT DROWNING FATALITY. FUNERAL OF DECEASED AND INQUEST. Impressive scenes were witnessed at the funeral of Mr. Fred Sparks, Stocks-lane, Penketh, who recently lost his life by drowning in the swimming bath at Penketh, which took place on Sunday afternoon, in the presence of a large gathering at the Sankey Cemetery. The procession from the house to St. Mary a Church, where the funeral service was held, was preceded by over 100 members of the Order of Druids, and included Bros, W. Woods (lodge secretory), H. Mainley (lodge treasurer), Deputy District Grand Master A. T. Clay, Past Grand Master D. Houghton, Messrs. James Dodds, J. T. Ambler. and T. FT. Ambler (Penketh Tanning Comnany), J. B. Aitken, Dr. Murray, Ethelbert Foster and W. Davies (honorary members). All the officers of the Order of Druids were present. Large numbers of the Orders of Reehabites and Free Gardeners followed the cortege. Iha bearers were : Messrs. G. Acomb, W. Broom, H. Jones, J. Hughes (companions), D. Atherton, E. Bond, T. Booth, N. Hatton (workmates), C. Monks, E. Rafters and J. Worsley (Druids). The choir rendered the 39th Psalm and the hymns " The saints on earth and those above "and "My God, my Father, while I stray" were sung. As the mourners lett the church the organist (Miss Standish) played the Dead M.treh in "Saul." The cortege was then conveyed from the church to the Cemetery. The Rev. J. R. Jones was the officiating clergyman. Large numbers of floral tributes were sent, including one from the Druids and the Penket'a Institute.

Daresbury. PRIMROSE LENGUE.—The members of the Daresbury Habitation of the Primrose League held their annual business meeting in the Sessions Room last Friday, Mr. R. I. Wynne Jones in the chair. The accounts were presented by the President in the absence of the Treasurer (Mr. J. E. Seeker), and showed a balance in hand of nearly £2. The following officers were elected : Dame President, Lady Greenall ; ruling councillor, Mr. R. I. Wynne Jones; hon. treasurer, Mr. Seeker ; and hon. secretary, Mr. Phillips. The Executive Council were re-elected en bloc with the addition of Mees-s. J. Wright and J. Ryder as new members. Messrs. C. Shepberd-Crtss and J. E. Seeker were appointed to serve on the Knutsford 'Divisional Council, and Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., was elected a new warden.

Padgate. Lord Wolmer Opens a- Garden Fete. The annual garden fete in connection with Christ Church, Padgate, vas beld,in the Vicarage grounds on Thursday afternoon and evening in blight' though windy, weather. The opening ceremony took place in a large tent. The Vicar, the Rev. G. W. Dickinson, presided, and was supported on the platform by Viscount Wolmer, who declared the fete open, Mr. H. N. Dickinson, Mr. James Critchley and Mr., E. W. C. London. Amongst others present were the Revs. Canon Willis, G. Vale Owen, B. Percival, J. H. G. Holling- worth, Parry Williams, Mis. Rylands, Mr. and Mrs. W. P. Rylands, Mr. and Mrs. John White, Mr. and Mrs. George Mather, Alderman and Mrs. Bennett, Mr. W. Bennett, Dr. and Mrs. Bennett,,Mr. and llrs. P. H. Bennett, Mr. and Mrs. Gitson, Mr. and Mrs. James Houghton, Mr. and Mrs. F. Wright, Mr. and Mrs. E. Dennett, Mrs. Dewburst, Miss Dewhurst (Birkdale), Mr. E. Allen, Mi. and Mrs. 11. Hoult and Mr. T. Johnson.

The Vicar said he would explain the objects of the annual fete. They had been troubled by dry-rot, and they had had the pews, the nave and the steeple repaired. Now the bill wanted paying, and it amounted to something like £BO. It was quite an extra expense on the parish. They also wanted to get rid of the quarterly collection, and they therefore wanted £129. There were decorations of the church to be seen to,end other improvements to be carried out. 'They made a record last year, and they tad got to make one this. He thought they could raise .£l7O or £lBO. He would now ask Lord Weimer to open the fete in a non-party attitude if the feelings were otherwise. Lord Weimer said they had got a most delightful day and a most delightful Garden. Mr. Dickenson had said that there was no Eve in the garden, and he (the speaker) hoped there was no serpent, for otherwise he was sure that it presented all the features of a more famous place. (Laughter). But if there were anything he could add lustre to the success that Mr. Dickenson had prepared it would be the tine assemblage of people who had turned up to help him in the cause, for which he had under- taken that fete. (Applause). "I think ladies and gentlemen," he went on "that these fetes are a most pleasant way of doing a most unpleasant business —that is to say,of getting money out of other peoples pockets. (Laughter). I know perfectly well that I am not allowed tok touch on politics this afternoon, and I assure you ladies and gentlemen, that I have no desire to do so, but I do wish that some of those kind dear people who are so anxious to dis- endower the church would take account of the strenuous efforts which the parish clergy are putting forth at the present moment to make both ends meet. If you will consider the great task that is before your Vicar at the present moment, and if you will think for a moment what efforts he has to make to keep the path h on a satisfactory footing you will tee, I think, that if our Church were disestablished and disendowed the ork would become almost impossible. And so, gentle- men, T think we can say that the establishment of the Church does not cripple the activities of the Church by over-glutting it with money. (Applause.) I declare this fete to be now open and I hope that the success of the day will continua as good as it has begun." (Applause). Mr. .James Critchley (people's warden) in proposing a vote of thanks to Lord Weimer, said lie would like the name of Lord Weimer to become a household word. They wanted the money for a noble cause. It was a beautiful little church. They wanted to keep it in good repair and if they could only get the money to do it, they could make it more beautiful still. He thought that if they would only look round they would see that the ladies meant to get the money. Mr. E. W. C. London, in seconding said that many of them had tried, to see the King on Tuesday and those who did, bad done what he had not. (Laughter). That garden fete was an auxiliary to the church collections and he hoped the money would be for, hcoming. The stallholders were as follows :—Refreshment stall Miss Jackson, Mrs. Denham, Mrs. Kerfoot,Mrs. Fryar, Misses Bowermg, Birchall, Birtles, N. and. F. Houghton, Denham, Roystc,n, and Warburton. Fancy stall : Mesdames Buckton, Blackwell, Allen, Haddock, Howard, Mather, Gorton, Royston, Walsh and Simpson. Rummage stall : Mesdames Young, Parrs, Povey, Burrell, Misses Wood, Heath and Brimelow. Flower stall : Misses K. and L. Birtles. Dip: E. Kerfoot and J. Simpson. Vicar's stall : Mr. and Mrs. T. Antrohus, jun., Mr. and Mrs. A. 0. Hilditch, -Mr. and Mrs. Gidenan, Mr. and Mrs. Atkinson, Mr. and Mrs. E. Atkinson, Mr. and Mrs. Vaughan. Sweet stall : Misses E. Berridge, Whitlow and L. Harter. Three excellent entertainments were provided by Messrs. Mertz and Whittle, of Albert Hall, South-. port. There was also the following competitions : Gentlemen's Hat -Trimming ; Ladies Washing • Gentle- rcen's Washing ; Whistling (ladies only) ; Ladies.and Gentlemen's Air Gun,Shooting.
The prizes were distributed by Viscount Wolmer.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

SAD DEATH OF A ST. HELENS TRADESMAN A painful sensation was created at St. Helens late on Thursday afternoon by the sudden death of Mr. John Edwards; plumber, of 213, Speakman-cad. Mr. Edwards was fifty years of age, and he had for many years been prominently connepted with the cricket and football clubs. On Thursday he was on the cricket ground untirfour o'clock in the afternoon. About twenty-five minutes past four Mr. Edwards was proceeding up the slope of Cowley Hill-lane from Bishop's-road, when a youth named Lancaster heard a crash. On looking round he sakw that Mr. Edwards had fallen off his bicycle in thle middle of the road. Assistance was at once .called, but before anything could be done the unfortunate cyclist had expired. Dr. Dow was quickly on the scene, and found that Mr. Edwards, who had apparently been in his usual health ten minutes before, was quite dead. He had a large bruise on the right temple, but death is supposed to have been brought about by sudden hemmorhage on the brain. Deceased leaves a widow and eight young children.

RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

At the monthly meeting of this Council, on Wednes- day, Mr. F. Wiswall, J.P., presiding, the medical officer reported that during June there were nineteen deaths and forty-six births, as comp:red with twenty .d.-aths and forty-one births in June of last year.—The .High- ways and Buildings Committee recommended the acceptance of an offer by the Highfleld Tanning Com- pany to allow the use of a field on the banks of the canal on which to deposit refuse. The minute was eventually passed.—Mr. R. H. Pringle wrote resigning his position as a msnager of Holy Trinity School, and Mr. Ralph Gibbs was appointed in his stead.—Mr. George H. Cox' Water-stree., Liverpool, and Mr. Herman J. Falk, Water-street, Liverpool, gave notice of their intention to apply to the Board of Trade for a provisional order under the Electric Lighting Acts authorising the supply of electricity for all public and private purposes within the urban district of Runcorn. —Mr. Handley said these gentltn:en represented the Salt,Union, Limited. Wright presided and there were also present :—Messrs. C. E. I.inaker (vice-chairman), C. E. Linaker, jun., W. Harrison, W. Nixon, J. 11. Davies, G. Pilhing, J. L. Jones, E. Egerton-Warburton, J. .• This committee repotted that they were prepared to give to the payment of 10s. (which they are to receive from Dr. W. H. Banks) towards the cost of the extension of the,sever in the main road in connection with the erection by Mr. D. Kirkham of eight semi- detached cottages on the Banks estate, providing the ssors and lessee, agreed to pay to the Council the remainder of the cost of such extension. The Clerk reported that the houses in Sandy-lane which were being erected by the Co-operative Society were now so advancel that it was necessary to consider the question of the extension of the sewer that for the present the sever be only extended to the first manhole. a distance of about four yards. div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
LABOUR DEMONSifrgION AT HAYDOCX SPEECHES BY MR. WILL CROOKS, M.P. AND MR. J. A. SEDDON, M.P. -

The annual great demonstration of miners and trades unionists organised by the Newton Division Labour Party was held on Saturday afternoon at Haydock Park. The different branches assembled at Ashton-in-Maker- field with seven brass bands, and then marched to the park, where speaking took place from'two platforms. About 10,000 trades unionists and workingmen were present. Mr. W. Speakman, of Newton presided at No. 1 platform. Mr. H. Twist moved a regolution urging the removal of the pauper disqualification and the reduction of the age limit for old age pensions, calling for immediate legislation giving the right to work, and rejoicing in the new sources of public revenue opened out by the land tf.sk and super-tax on big incomes as being" the only true fiscal reform consistent with Free Trade which the workers can support." Mr. W. Davies seconded. - - -

Will Crooks, M.P., supported the resolution in a characteristic speech which frequently convulsed the audience. Be said they were that day celebrating their independence. He wished they all felt independent. The everlasting dread of what they were going to do when they got old, of what the children were going to do if father broke down, the everlasting worry of a workman's home would make men fight to give real independence 'to people who deserved it most of all. Labour legislation had gone -a long way in the House of Commons. If the working men only realised his power he would alter the government of the country in twenty-four hours. He promised that the Labour party would attend to the matter of the pauper disqualification for old-age pensions. He claimed that under Free Trade the 'land of the country could give work for all. All the houses, shops and factories covered 600,000 acres, and there were 47:000,000 acres ; 250,000 men owned' or they had got 44,000,010 acres, and 38,000,000 people had got Lone—and those people were the sovereign people. the bulwark of a gleat mpite on which the sun never set. hat swank. (Loud laughter). Was a Tariff Reformer there ? With all that land they 'could grow enough stuff for all the people. Germany impoited 7s. per head of the popula- tion in foodstuffs. England imports ,£4 per head or £172,000,000 a year. It could be grown here. Tariff Reform-Chloroform ! (Loud and continued laughter). What rot the "We want eight and we won't

'wait" cry was. When Tariff Reform was first started Mr. Chamberlain said, "What you want to do is to put. 10 per cent. duty on goods coming in. That would realise £10.000,000. If the industrial community so desire I could give old-age pensions with that; but it will do more, it will keep the good out, and that will make more work at home." If he kept them out how did be get the £10,000,090 for bringing them in? That w..nted a bit of doing,even by Lancashire trea.(Laughter). No wonder their opponents objectei to tne pudic- houses being shut on polling day. The more muddled the people were the bet.er they liked it. Did they (the working Hen) think that if Tariff Reform meant more trade for the workers they would be against it? They knew the Labour party would be for it, and when people said " Give it a trial," the trial would 'mean staving men, women, and.children' and not as long as he had breath in his body would he be for it. (Loud and continued applause). Mr. T. Glover, M.P., spoke at length on the Miners' Eight Hours Bill, and denied that it would reduce at all seriously the output of coal. He believed it would give more employment. MR. SEDDON ON TORY " LIES." •

Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P. for Newton, was most cordi- ally received, and expressed his unbounded gratification at the overwhelming success of the demonstration There was a Prima se League demonstration in that district, and he thought some of them out of curiosity might lave wanted to see the youth who had come to do tattle in the constituency. in connection with the campaign of Lord Wolmer, he bad had forwarded to him some of the leaflets that were distributed at his meet- ings, and he found they not only eot a noble lort, but tbey Lad got a few liars as well. In the country districts some very pretty fairy tales had been circulated. At Moss Bank the leaflet said, " Under Free Trade in England our workhouses are full Under Tariff Reform .smerica has no need of work- houses." A day or two before he met at a labour con- fez ence the president of the American Federation of Labour, and he was startled by\this statement, and said that in New York County they had a permanent ' destitute population of nearly 15,0003 and in every other State, from the Pacific to the Atlantic, there were as many poor destitute people as they could find in any other crvilked country. The second lie was, " Under Free Trade in England beer is heavily taxed ; tobacco is taxed heavily. In Tariff Reform Germany beer carries no tax ; tobacco is not taxed." He bad recently been in Germany, and he had to pay 3d. more for two ounces of tobacco than at home, lie had in his tand the proposed scale of new _taxation in Germany, and he found that the increased tax to be put on beer was 100,000,000 marks, on spirits 83,000,000 marks, on tobacco 43,000,000 marks, tea and coffee 57,000,000 marks spsrkling wine 5,000,000 marks. (Laughter.) That slowed them how false the Tory leaflet was. Speaking of the opposition to the Budget, he said he believed in the brotherhood of man, and he had Dever said anything al-out. the alien; tut be w. nted to tell Lord Rothschild and all those who had grown rich in this country, if they were prepared to stand in the way of justice and equity so far as taxation was concerned, then be was prepared to attack them as strorgly as he possibly could. He was prepared to welcome and sup- port the Budget, because it was the first clarion note that a Chancellor of the Exchequer was prepared to lead the industrial army into their rightful possession— the land of their birth. (Applause). , The resolution was unanimously carried. Mr. T. Watson presided at the tecoud platform, where Mr. Crooks and Mr. Seddon also spoke,and an interest- ing address was given by Mr. S. Walsh, M.P. for Ince.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
Relieving Officers Appointed.

The fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, the Rev. T. R. Matthews presiding. There were also present :=Mrs. Simps,n, Mrs, Collingwood, Miss Broadbent. Rev. M. Ryan, Dr. Murray, Messrs. G. Mather' A. J, Jolly, E. L. Bent, J. Evans, W. Gill, R. Bolton, R. Lee, W. Furness, J. Billinge, T. Ritchie, M. W. seton' W. Flanmsg in, .7. Cook, P. Longton, J. 8311, A. Brooks, A. Bottomley (clerk), R. W. Peacock (assistant clerk), J. F. Awbery (master), and A. Wright (tuperintendent of the Cottage Homes).
DR. CORKER'S ILLNESS.

The CLERK read a report by the medical officer (Dr. A. Hocigkinson) to the effect that Dr. Corker, the assistant resident medical officer, was not progressing as nipidly as they would like and he would not be able to resume his duties before the end of July. In order that the work of the institution might be carried en in a satisfactory manner a locum. tenens was necessary. Mr. BILLINGE expressed the regret of the 13)ard at the continued illness of Dr. Corker. He had unfortu- nately contracted poisoning in the eya while attending to a patient. •
The matter WAS referrad to the House Comm itter.. Dr. Hodgkinson •being empowered to make provisional arrangemen's for a locum. tentos.
SUBSCRIPIION TO THE INFIRMARY.
On the recommenchtion of the Financ Committee, it was decided to increase the liolrd's annual subscrip- tion to the Warring'on Intirmary from £2O to 30 guineas.

div.head: RELIEVING OFFICERS AEPOINTF.D.
div.p: RELIEVING OFFICERS AEPOINTF.D.

The Board then proceeded to the appointment of two relieving officers. Out-of over nicety applications, the following six candidates had Leen selected to appear before the Board :—Ernest Harry Cotterill,farm bailiff, Acton Grange; Maurice Joseph Cox, Police-constal le, 51, Oxford-street; Thomas Richard Dennett, police clerk, 23, Oxfo,d-s:reet ; Frederick Gidman, book keeper an confidential clerk. Padgate-lane ; Ernest A. Sanders, solicitor's' clerk, 239, Lovely-lane ; _John Newton Vernon, accountant and rent collector, 52, Wilkicsen-etreet. The CLERK informed 111(‘ Board that the Local Government Board were acting on the recommendation of the Poor Law Commission not to appoint anybody as a relieving officer who had not previously held the position of assistant relieving officer or i+ho did not possess a certain certificate. If the Board made an appointment that morning he would have to repost it to the Local Governm nt Board and the chances were that they would not be prepared to approve it.

• The Rev. M. RYAN: I take it that recommendation has not been acted upon yet in any case. The CLERK: Yes, it has. The Local Government Board have objected to anprovin; an appointment within the last few months. The Guardians could appoint whom they thought fit and he would do his utmost to try to get the Local Government Board to approve the appointment. The CRAIRMAN : You don't encourage us with the assurance that the person whom we appoint will be accepted by the Local Government Bosrd. The CLERK: Ido not, under the circumstances.

Mr. BILLTNGE ; I suppose the probabilities an that if the selected persons tundertake to qualify withia certain time, the Local Government Board may probably under those conditions approve the appointment. The Board then interviewed the selected candidates, and it was rlecided to appoint Messrs. Ernest Harry Cotterill and Frederick Gidman, subject to the approval of the Local Government Board.

Mr. Registnr Atichison, on Wednesday at the Manchester County Court, made a receiving., order on the debtors' petition agrinst Mr. Thomas Whitelegg o f Barns-lane Farm, Warburton, Farmer. Mr. Thomas S. Steel, solicitor, Warrington, appeared for the debtor.

div.head: ROYAL VISIT.
div.p: THE ROYAL VISIT.
WHY THE CAR WAS CLOSED.
The Cost of the Present and the
Decorations.
The Thanks of their Majesties.
DRINCESS VICTORIA WEARS THE DIAMOND
NECKLACE
The following letters have been received by . the Mayor from Mr. Haldane '(Secretary for War), the Minister in attendance on their Majesties on Tuesday. Knowsley, Prescot, • 6th July, 1009.

Dear Mr. Mayor,— I am eommanded by the King to express the pleasure which his visit to Warrington of this afternoon has given him, and to say to you that his Majesty was much gratified by the cordial welcome given not only-by yourself and the Corporation, but by the people, to himself and to the Queen. Believe me, yours faithfully, R. B. HALDANE.

Knowsley, Prescot, 6th July, 1909. Dear Mr. Mayor,—l am commanded by Her Royal Highness, Princess Victoria, to convey to you her -warm appreciation-of the gift of a'diamond necklace, which was made to her this afternoon from Warring- ton. Her Royal Highness was deeply touched by the thoughtfulness of those who remembered her birthday in this kindly fashion. I may mention that she took the earliest opportunity of showing her feeling for the gift by wearing the diamonds this evening. Believe me yours faithfully, R. B. HALDANE.

div.head: Letters from the Mayor,
div.p: Letters from the Mayor,
(To THE EDITOR OF THE " EXAMINER ")
9th July 1909.

Sir,—May I take this opportunity of thanking 'through your columns th 6 inhabitants of Warrington for the hearty response they made to my request for decorations. I should like also to say , that I was extremely struck with the orderly behaviour of the people lining the route. WM. J. FASHAW, Mayor.

div.head: TO THE EDITOR OF THE " EXAMINER."
div.p: TO THE EDITOR OF THE " EXAMINER."

Sir.--I hear from all sides that _there was the keenest disappointment on Tuesday, at the great pace at which their Majesties travelled through the town. It was certainly promised that, if the weather permitted, their Majesties would ride in an open car; but I am given to understand that when their Majesties left Worsley the weather 'tvas . so bad that this could not be expected. When, however, the people had expended money and labour in making the town as beautiful as possible, and had waited patiently for hours, not out of idle curiosity, but for the purpose of showing their loyalty, I can not only understand but also share their dis- appointment when the Royalty, whom they were so eager to welcome, passed by almost unseen. I desire, however, to say that his Majesty expressed to me that he was deeply -touched with the loyalty dislayed by the people of this town, and I feel sure that it could not have' been the wish of their Majesties to.be taken through the town at such a speed as to be invisible except to a few.—Yours faithfully, WILLIAM J. FORSHAW, Mayor. Warrington, 9th July, 1909.

div.head: Why the Royal Car was Closed.
div.p: Why the Royal Car was Closed.

We are informed on good authority that.at the Lord Mayor of Liverpool's reception on Wednesday the Earl of Derby made allusion to the proceedings at Warrington. He, Said that their Majesties were absolutely charmed. with the town and the decora- tions., arid would certainly have passed through in an open car but for the fact that the Queen was suffering from neuralgia.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE " EXAMINER"."

Sir,—lt may possibly interest your readers to know that, in accordance with a suggestion made to the Earl of Derby by one or two personal friends of Mr. William Stewart Royston, of Springfield:Paddington, their Majesties " slowed down specially, on passing his house. in order that Mr. Royston, who is a great sufferer and has been confined to his room for many years, might have an opportuuity of seeing them; and that Mr. Royston was much gratified to receive a salute from the King as the Royals Motor glided slowly by. I am told that most of the other inhabitants of Paddington (which was prettily decorated for the occasion) were equally fortunate, and had an excellent view of the Royal party. Lord Derby has since written to Mr. Royston to express his regret that he was not able to see more of their Majesties " owing to the motor being closed," and explains that this was " rendered: necessary by, the very severe neuralgia from which her Majesty was suffering.". The fact may possibly do something to explain the general disappointment on Tuesday, and may help to modify the hasty judgments passed by many of my townsfolk on the Royal Visit.— Faithfully yours,
ARTHUR BEN.NETT. Paddington House, near Warrington, 9th July, 1909.
The text of Lord Derby's letter, which reached Mr. Royston on Thursday, was a follows : , Knowsley, . .7 Prescot, Lancs. 7th July, 1909.

Dear did slow down the motors in passing your house, but I am afraid you could not have seen very much of their Majesties owing to the motors being closed, which was rendered necessary by the very severe neuralgia from which her Majesty was suffering
Yours faithfully, DERBY.

div.head: IV. Stewart Royston, Esq. A Complaint About the Expense.
div.p: IV. Stewart Royston, Esq. A Complaint About the Expense.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE " EXAMINER. Sir,—The King and Queen have come and gone. We are glad to have had them in our midst, and have the pleasant recollection of having seen them—at any rate we who were so fortunate. But there remains the bitter sting of being compelled to pay without saying yea or nay for .a lot of unnecessary decoration. If ever there was a time when rigid economy should be practised by the rate- spenders, it is the present, after the long spell of bad trade which has not yet finished. There are those who are coming constantly for bread, not casual tramps, but our own townspeople who are destitute; and these, like all cottage dwellers, will have to con- tribute their quota in the rates, to the hundreds of _pounds wasted I say on decoration. I am confident that the King did not desire the display that was made, (if he knew it), ; and if he knew how it had been done, and the condition of the people mho were forced to help to pay for it. His 'Majesty would be the first to repudiate it. And the diamond necklace ! We read in the news reports, that this present was made on behalf of the Corporation. I trust that it means that various mem- bers of the Council have subscribed privately for it. If not I hope that more will be heard about it from more influential and abler men than myself. The Council met and voted £1,200 to the Mayor for his expenses, as coally no doubt, as they would partake of a cup of tea. I doubt if that sum will cover half the expense incurred. The funds for decoration ought to have been raised by public subscription, and then the burden would have fallen-on those only who had money to spare. The Councillors responsible have broken a public trust. They are the trustees of the ratepayers, a great bulk of whom are in very poor circumstances, and the sooner they realise their duty, the better.-- am yours truly,
JOHN RICHARDSON. 114, Buttermarket-street, Warrington. July Bth, 1909.

div.head: Tribute to the Crowd.
div.p: A Tribute to the Crowd.

One of the most pleasing features of the great occasion on Tuesday was the orderliness of the crowd all along the route over which the Royal.party passed after entering the Borough, and the Chief Constable wishes us to place on record his sincere appreciation of the exemplary manner in which the thousands of Warrington people conducted themselves throughout a long period of waiting. No report of any robbery was received, and there were no cases of disorder for the magistrates to adjudicate upon the folowing day .

div.head: Guard of Honour Entertained.
div.p: Guard of Honour Entertained.

On Thursday evening the men of the 4tli Battalion Prince of Wales's Volunteers South Lancashire Regi- ment who comprised the Ruard--of-honour on the occasion of the Royal visit to Warrington, were enter- tained to A hot pot supper in the Drill Hall. Captain H. G. Roberts (who commanded the guard-of-honour( presided, and the other officers of the batalion in attendance were ;—Colonel J. D. Fairclough (com- manding officer). Captains It. Smith, Owen, Cary and Avery,. Lieutenants McClure, Adams, Whittle and Skinner, and Sergeant Major Ingram. The Mayor (Alderman Forshaw) was also present, The toast of ! The King" was honoured on the proposition of the Chairman.—Colottel Fairclough proposed the health of the Mayor, and in responding the Mayor thanked the assembly for the kind way -in which they had received him i and said he was very proud of the battalion and of the way in which they acquitted them- selves at the Royal review. He referred to the splendid reception which the battalion had .at Liver- pool and to the appreciative way in which the Brigadier spoke of them. His Worship concluded by saying he would do all in his power to assist the Corps. —During the _evening a capital musical programme was submitted,- the artistes including Mr. Billy Williams, comedian from the Hippodrome. AN ACCIDENT.

Whilst waiting to see the King. on Tuesday, Patrick McLachlear,lB, Ship Yard,- was injured.. It appear t that he was supporting himself against the fountain near Holy Trinity Church, when a man wish- ing to obtain a good view of the passing motors attempted to get to the top of the foUntain. In doing so he grasped the head piece which broke off and fell on to the lad's hand, badly crushing two of his ,fingers. lie was taken to the Infirmary, where the little finger at the middle joint was amputated.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

THE GARDEN SOCIETV—The memters of the Steck-ton Heath Garden Society were given the oppor- tunity on Thursday evening of visiting the grounds, gardens and stables of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., at Walton Hall, and over a hundred availed themselves of the privilege. They were highly delighted IN ith the visit. Tbe gardens were apparently at their hest, while the visitors derived the greatest pleasure in being allowed to roam about the beautiful grounds. The stables, c., aroused the undisguised admiratlon of the party quite as much as the striking floral features of Walton Hall. On Saturday, the junior section of the Society had the privilege of rambling over the groundsand gardens, and were much impressed with the visit. The attractions of the vinery, it is said, proved a strong temptation to some of the younger members of the-party, but they tried to content them- selves by the said reflection that the grapes were sour. Lady Greenall met several of the children and shook bands with them. Sir Gilbe; t is this year's president of the Society and Lady Greenall has kindly consented to open the summer show to be held in Hill Caffe Park on the 21st August.

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL BUSINESS.
div.p: TOWN COUNCIL BUSINESS.
The July meeting of the Town Council will be held on Tuesday evening. • Mr. Fl. It ober; swill be officially returned as Councillor for Whitecross Ward.

Alderman Tinnion has a special resolution for the purpose of relegating the business of notices of motion to the end of the Council meetings instead of considering it before the minutes of Committees as at present.

div.head: SENIORITY.
div.p: SENIORITY.

Councillor Wilkinson proposes to substitute the Standing Order as to seniority by one specifying uninterrupted tenure of office, but an interval not exceeding fifteen months is not to be considered an interruption of tenure.

div.head: CATHOLICS AND WALKING DAY.
div.p: THE CATHOLICS AND WALKING DAY.

At a meeting of the Watch Committee a letter was read from the Rev. J. P. Whittle complaining of the arrangements made by the Chief Constable for the procession on Walking Day. Resolved, that the arrangements made by the Chief Constable be approved, and that the Town Clerk intimate to the Rev. Father Whittle that this Commsttee are not prepared to n ake any alteration in such arrangements.

div.head: CLOSING OF INSNNITARY HOUSES. _ _ _
div.p: CLOSING OF INSNNITARY HOUSES. _ _ _

The Health Committee has resolved that the Town Clerk be instructed to take the necessary proceedings under the Housing of the Working Classes Act, 1890-3, for the closing of houses numbered 1, 3 and 5, Richard son's Court, which have teen reported by the Medical Officer of Health to be unfit for human babitati(n.

div.head: BATHING FOR LADIES.
div.p: BATHING FOR LADIES.

The Baths Committee has resolved that the Ladies Swimming Bath be opened on Thursday morning at the reduced charge or 2d. per bather, and also in the afternoon if not required by ths Eduction Committee.
SLOT METERS.

Councillor Broadhurst will ask how many slot meter consumers have benefited by the reduction in the price of gas, and when the whole of the consumers'vrill, at the present rate, be benefiting by the reduction.

div.head: WARRINGTON CYCLING CLUB,
div.p: WARRINGTON CYCLING CLUB,

The bowling meeting with the Warrington Commercial Travellers Association at Hunts Cross on the 26th ult., proved in every way a great success and an enjoyable fixture. The travellers, together with a number of the club members, made the journey by rail, while the cycling section got away early in the afternoon and reached the destination shortly after the train party. The bowling competition between the two parties was started early in the afternoon and caused great interest. The bowling resulted in the travellets scoring in the singles an aggregate of 157 against the clubs 181, and in the doubles 82 against the clubs 80, the travellers thus winning the match by 33. A large number sat down to tea at the Hunts Cross Hotel and speeches of a con- gratulary nature as to the enjoyment of the attertoon followed, with -wishes for future meetings. On Friday, the 2nd inst., a section of Wheelers again made the journey to Hunt's Cross and had an enjoyable afternoon on the green.

The Walking Day week-end to Chester and Farnden was well attended. The party left headquarters early on Ssturday . afternoon and after a stay for tea in Chester proceeded to Farmion, where a pleasant week- end was spent. The return home was made on the Sunday evening.

The- bowling-competitions at Sankey are going along satisfactorily. On Wednesday evening tie find for the cup competition was played off, and resulted in Nr. James Houghton winning the trophy for the current year. The consolation handicaps are now also in the final stages, and the competition will probably be finished in a few weeks.

_ • The inter-club run with St. Helens C.C. to Dunham Massey on Thursday evening was favoured by fine weather and excellent roads. There was a respectable turn-out and the run proved an enjoyable fixture. The Club's arrangements fo'r the current week are : To-day's visit to the Club's president, Mr. John Naylor at Beeston Towers. Members travelling by rail can obtain return tickets via Chester at 2s. BS. Bowling at Sankey on Wednesday; Thursday, run to Hon Green.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
Clarke—Peers

At the Warrington Parish Church on Tuesday, the marriage took place of Mr. William T. Clarke, son of Mr. W. Clarke, son of Mr. W. Clarke, of Wellfield- street, and Miss Elizabeth Peers, daughter of the late Mr. John Peers, 7, Church-street. The ceremony was performed by the Rector (Rev. Canon Willis). The bride, who was given away by her step-father (Mr. J, W, Mortors), wore a bealatifial dress of rale , cream silk with hat to match,.and oftiried a shower bouquet of white lilies and smilax. The, bridesmaids were Miss C. Duckworth and-Miss C. Clarke (sister. of the bridegroom) and they were attired in pale blue striped voile with black picture hats. Their bouquets were comsosed of sweet peas and smilax. Mr. Albert Leigh, of Grappenhall, acted as best man. The reception was held at 7, Church-street, a large number of relatives and friends attending. Later the newly- married couple left for Llandudno, where the honey- moon will be spent. They were the recipients of many beautiful presents.

div.head: Hawthorn —Campbell.
div.p: Hawthorn —Campbell.

The marriage was solemnized at Wycliffe Congrega- tional Church on Wednesday afternooo, Of Mr. Charles Edward Hawthorn, third . son of the late. Thomas Hawthorn, 27, Lovely-lane, Warrington, and Miss Elsie Campbell, daughter of Mr, John Fa. ulkes Campbell, 67, Marshhouse-lane, Warrington.. The Rbv. John Yonge officiated. Mr: W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac., was at the organ and played choice- selections, including Mendelssohn's wedding march. The bride, who was given away by her father, was charmingly attired in a robe of cream silk mohair shannin with cream bat to match, and carried a bouquet -a white lilies and roses. • , She was attended by two bridesmaids, Mis 3 F. Wright of LisCard, and Miss M. Hawthorn (sister of the . bridegroom), whose dresses were of Wedgewood blue, eolienne, trimmed with lace, with black picture hats. They carried bouquets of pink carnations, the gifts of the bridegi oom. Mr. Joseph Hawthorn (brother of the bridegroom) discharged the duties of best man. After the ceremony a reception was held in the Wycliffe Memorial Buildings, and later The happy couple left for Scarborough where the honeymoon is .being spent. The bride's travelling dress was a mole costume. Numerous handsome presents were received.

div.head: Hobbs —Brandreth.
div.p: Hobbs —Brandreth.

A very pretty wedding was solemnized at the Church of St. Mary Magdalene,Ashton-on-Mersey. The contract- ing parties were Miss Florence Hobbs, only daughter of Mr. and • Mrs. Hobbs, of Holly Bank, Dunbar-lane, Ashton-on-Mersey, and Mr. Robert Gorst Brandreth, eldest son of Mr. and Mrs. Robert Gorst Brandieth, of Padgate-lane, Warrington. The bridegroom is well- known in Warrington, being an official of the Warring- ton Corporation. (gas department), secretary of the Warrington Football Association, and secretary of the Parish Church Men's Bible Class. He is also well known in Friendly Societies, being a Past Grand of the Constitution Lodge ,Independent Order of Odd- fellows (Manchester Unity). The bride, who carried a bouquet of white •foses, the gift of the bridegroom, was gowned in ivory duchesse satin with wreath and veil decorated with orange blossom. The bridesmaids *(Miss Mabel Brown, cousin of the bride, • and Miss Jennie Brandreth, sister of the) bridegroom) were prettily attired in emboidered muslin and wore black picture hats. They carried bouquets of mauve sweet peas, and wore gold and pearl brooches, the gifts of the bridegrooni. The bride's mother was dressed in black satin 'With hat to match, and carried a bouquet of crimson roses. The, bridegroom's mother wore grey crepe de Chene and carried a bouquet of crimson roses and maiden-hair fern... The bride was given away by her. father. Mr. W. J. Hopkins officiated as•best man and Mr. Thomas Hopkins capably fulfilled the duties of groomsman. The officiating clergyman was the Rev.. F. M. Price. After the ceremony a receptiOn was held at the house of the brlde's father where the wedding breakfast was partaken Of. Later in the day' the happy couple left for North Wales where the honeymoon will be spent. The bride's travelling costume was a brown material with hat .to match trimmed with cherry coloured velvet.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRIP DAY.
div.p: WARRINGTON TRIP DAY.
Siturday was Warrington's annual trip day and the employees at the various works spent a pleasant time at popular seaside resorts.
CORPORATION GO TO BLACKPOOL.

The Corporation employees visited Blackpool on Saturday. About 500 journeyel by special train which left Bank Quay Station at 6.50 a.m. The arrangements provided free almission to the Tower and this W 43 fully taken adyantigs of. Warrington was reached at 8 30 in the evening. , ARNIITAGE AND RIGBY'S VISIT SOUIIIPORT.

Southport was this year the rendezvous of 1,500 people who went with Armitage and Rigby's trip. Three special trains of the 'Cheshire Lines Railway conveyed thorn to their destination and the thy was spent in the midst of brilliant sunshine. Many of the workpeople spent their holidays at Southport the works at Warrington having been stopped for 10 days. The workpeople, who have bad a savings, club, inaugur- ated in connection with the trip, divided £250 between them.

div.head: CO-OPERATIVE TRIP TO LONDON.
div.p: CO-OPERATIVE TRIP TO LONDON.

Over 200 members and friends of the Warrington Equitable Industrial Co-operative Society,journeyed to London last Saturdly roorning,departing from Warring- ton Central Station at 12.!.30 a.m.Soon after 5 o'clock they arrived at Luton where they had breakfast. Before leaving at 9.15 for London they visited the OAKS. Cocoa Works and watched the various processes with interest London was reached soon after 10 o'clock and inn. road party went for a drive, proceeding along Gray's road to High Holborn,Nev+gate-streett past Old Bailey (late Newgate Prison), St. Martin's-le-Grand, Cheapside, for St. Paul's. They then paid a visit to St. Paul's Cathedral and were much impressed with the magnificence of the building. The drive was then resumed, going along Cannon-street, Queen Victoria-street, past the Mansion House Bank of England, along King William- street, past the Monument, over London Bridge,Tooley- street, and the Tower Bridge. On their arrival at the Tower Bridge the visitors were pleased to see it in use, a steamer passing,underneath at the time. In the Tower they saw the Crown Jewels and regalia. After such a long drive it will readily ba seen that the party's appetites must have been whetted, and dinner was served at six o'clock at the C.W.S. Cafe, Leman-street. Dinner over the drive was resumed, and they went past the Royal Mint, Minories, to Aldgate, along Leadenhall- street to Bank, Cheapside, past the Guildhall, Bow Church (of Dick Whittingt°' fame), St. Martins-le-Grand, Ludgate Hill, along the Thames Embankment, to Westminster. It was a source of satisfaction to find that service was in pro- gress when they reached the Abbey. The party entered the Palace of Westminster, visiting both Houses. The drive was then proceeded with, going along White- hall, Horse Guards, Charing Cross, Trafalgar Square, Pall Mall, past Marlborough House to Buckingham Palace, along Constitution Hill to Hyde Park, Albert Memorial, Albert Hall, along Knightsbridge, Picaadilly. on to the Imperial International Exhibition, Speherds' Bush. Tea was enjoyed at the Exhibiticn Banquet Hall Garden Club. 'The party left St. Pancras Station at 12.30 Sunday morning reaching Warrington, about 6 o'clock. Praise is due to Messrs. W. Haigh B. Farrar and G. T. Rushton who superintended the outing.

WILLIAM ROBERTSON, LTD., LATCHFORD. The seventh annual picnic of the employees of the above company took place on Saturday last, the destination again being Blackpool. About 130 took part in the excursion. Two special cars conveyed the party from Latchford to Warrington, and a start was made from Bank Quay at 6.15 a.m. Blackpool was reached by 8 a.m. and though the morning was some- what dull, the air was keen, and conducing to a good appetite for the dinner which was served in the Victoria Hall at the Winter Gardens at 11.30 a.m. Mr. Wareing (the manager), and Mrs. Wareing, "and Mr. Collins (the secretary), and Mrs. Collins were present at this function, and Mr. Wareing read a telegram from Mr. Robertson (the chairman of the company), expressing the great regret of himself and Mrs. Robertson in not being able to be with them on the present occasion. Addressing a few words to the company, Mr. Wdreing hoped that they would all make the best of the day, and get as much enjoyrnent out of it as possible. He thought that thanks were due to Mr. Collins and Mr. Humphreys for their management of the picnic, and also to the members of the office staff who had assisted them in the work. Mr. Collins replied, and on behalf of the WorkpeoPle expressed regret at the unavoidable absence ,this time of Mr. and Mrs. Robertson. They were very pleaged however that Mr. and Mrs. Wareing had been able to be present. The organisation of this annual excursion had certainly entailed a considerable amount of work, but both Mr. Humphreys and he were amply repaid by the knowledge of the pleasure consequent upon it. This was the seventh annual picnic, aud each one seemed to witness a further step of progress .of the company. The Workmen's Sick Club was ;n a very healthy condition, practically every man now being a m.ember, A considerable sum of money has also been

put by during the year in the Workmen's Saving Club. He hoped that during the coming year thee institu- tions would be as successful as in the past, and that we should meet next year in enhanced numbers. During the afternoon the weather was fine, but after tea it broke somewhat. However, the party was fortunate in having arranged for admission throughout the day to the Winter Gardens, where many sought refuge coupled with amusement. The return journey was commenced at nine, and Warrington was reached 4 safely by 11.

div.head: TORIES AT B.RIDGE FOOT.
div.p: TORIES AT B.RIDGE FOOT.
Lord Wolmer on Food Taxation.

• The unique spectacle of a real live lord holding forth to the multitude at Bridge Foot was responsible for a large gathering at the open-air meeting organized by the Conservatives of Warrington in celebration of Mr. Chamberlain's birthday on Thurs- day evening. The youthful. Lord Wolmer, who IS trying to oust Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P. from the representation of Newton division, was the principal speaker and on the platform were :—Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., who presided, Mr. and Mrs. Robert Pierpoint, Mr. AV. P. Rylands, Alderman Bennett, Councillors Fulton Smith, Broadhurst, and 'Wilson, Mr. W. L. Williams, and Mr. H. N. Dickinson. Judging from the running fire of interjections, the audience included many tho were not in sympathy with the views- expounded: • TheenAza MAN said the meeting had been happily called for that day which was the anniversary of the birth of one of our greatest and most noble statesmen, Mr. Joseph Chamberlain. Lord WOLM ER, who speaks with distinctness and deliberation, said that whatever political- party they belonged to, there were very few people who did not admire the personality of Mr. Chamberlain. (Hear, hear.) They admired the strenuous life of that great man, and they admired the unflinching courage he showed which made him go straight to the people when- ever be had made up his mind on any great question. He thought Mr. Chamberlain's great strength lay in the fact that he was not only a statesman and idealist but also a businessman. (Hear' hear.) Dealing with the present conditions under "free imports," Lord Wolmer said the man who sot up a factory abroad had the foreign market secured to him and the English- market open to to him, while the man who set up a factory in England had the foreign market closed to him and he had to fight for his uwo existence, even at home. If Mr. Chamberlain considered Tariff Reform necessary six years ago, it was much more necessary to-day. Capitalists were exporting their capital to foreign countries more and more, and when it was pointed out to Mr. Asquith that capital was being taken abroad, he replied that the exportation of capital was a healthy symptom, and he added "Long may it continue." But so long as it continued, said Lord Weimer, the people who took that capital abrcad would be employing foreigners instead of Englishmen. That was what Tariff Reform was to stop. They wished to give the British worker a preference over the foreign worker. It was because Tariff Reform was a national policy, that it was going to be endorsed by the people of the country. A few months ago when the mother country was in need of ships the people of the Colonies came. forward and offered three Dreadnoughts. We knew perfectly well that one nation was building Dreadnoughts in rivalry to our fleet and the question for us to settle was whether we were going to do trade with the people who built Dreadnoughts against us or with those who built Dreadnoughts for us. (Applause.) Their opponents sometimes said that if we were to give the Colonies a preference it would be necessary to tax the food of the people. -That statement was absolutely untrue. Free Traders had taken a eel tain statement of 'Mr. Chamberlain's about putting A TAX ON THE PEOPLE'S FOOD

and they had isolated it from the rest of his speeches and made a perfectly misleading and unjust use of it. What tariff reformers proposed to do as not to add a single penny to the food taxation of the people. Under our system of Free Trade the food of the people was taxed to the tune of £13,000,000. Tarift Reformers promised that for every penny they put on wheat or meat that was imported from foreign countries they were going to take an equal amount off tea,

coffee, sugar and cocoa which were taxed at the present time. They pledged themselves that they were not going to add a single penny to the food taxes of the people, and the cry that they wished to do so was nothing short of an absolute lie. He ventured to say that before many months had passed, the people' of this country, who were tired of a system which deliberately encouraged unemployment, would give the principles of tariff reform a fair chance and adopt a national policy like every other country in the world had adopted. (Applause.) Mr. PIERPOINT said that the prosperity of other countries had increased enormously under their system of tariffs, and he saw no reason why this country, for the sake of an old shibboleth and an exploded idea, should continue under a policy under which there were so many men absolutely without work and the means of life. Dealing with food taxation, Mr. Pierpoint said that what was proposed was that certain taxes of a very low order should be put maialy on foreign wheat, and if that had any effect, which was doubtful, even if they paid the whole tax of 2s. a quarter it would not amount to more than a farthing on the 41b. loaf. What did it matter to them if sufficient was taken off other things they consumed, to equal and more than equal the farthing on the loaf? Mr. PierpOint denounced the Budget as Confiscatory, but a voice in the audience. chimed in with the remark that it was a "workingman's Budget." Mr. Pierpoint- contended tint the Budget and the Finance Bill embodied a Land Bill and an Anti-Brewers and Publicans' 13111, which had been introduced in a spirit of revenge. By long custom it was not expected that the House of Lords would alter a money Bill, but when that money Bill included practically a Land Bill and a Licensing Bill, it might be that the Lords would think it right to interfere. (Interruptions). He asked the audience as sensible men : What objection had they to the House of Lords? (A Voice: "Every objec tion.") One of the bases of the freedom of their country was that every man had a right t 3 trial by jury. The House of Lords, to his mind, was there like so many jurors to judge on a question and it was perfectly cer- tain that when the country had made up its mind on a question the House of Lords would never stand in the way of the people. He hoped very much that the Bill would be so changed in the House of Commons that the Lords would not have to exercise their undoubted legal right. (Applause). Mr. W. Y. RYLANDS, in moving a vote of thanks to the speakers, also had a tilt at the Budget. He observed that if money was to be found a large income tax was a way to find it. He personally favoured tariff reform, but supposing the people of this country were against tariff reform and must have the money, then he was,not prepared to .say there was anything wrong about the income tax. But he wanted them clearly to understand that any increase in the inpome tax which had to be paid by one section of the community reduced the spending power of that section and to that extent it reduced the amount of money that was distributed in the form of wages. The effect of taxation upon land would be so to cripple the landed proprietors, a great many of whom were hard put to it to keep their estates in the finest possible condition, that they would be compelled to reduce the staffs which they employed, on those estates and the efficiency sc ith which they kept up their farms, and the rural population would have to bear the brunt. He claimed that tariff reform would not only raise revenue, but provide employment for the people and the wherewithal to pay for food taxes and the like. (Applause). Alderman BENNETT, in seconding, paid a tribute to the memory of the late Councillor Nield, who was sincerely devoted to the cause of tariff reform. In the course of a eulogy of Mr. Chamberlain, the speaker said .it was be who first lit the flame which eventuated in the policy of old-age pensions. (Some dissent).He was prepared to maintain anywhere in regard to the great boon of old-age pensions which had recently been given by the Liberal Government, that the germ of that idea and the primary motive came from the fertile mind of Mr. Chamberlain. The vote of thanks was carried and it was also agreed to send a telegram congratulating Mr. Chamberlain on

his 73rd birthday. - Councillor BROADHURST moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman. Mrs. PEARSON, a representative of the Women's Unionist and Tariff Reform Association, who seconded, prophesied that in the days to come there would be a statue erected in every town of the size of Warrington to the memory of Mr. Chamberlain and that the inscription would be "He taxed the food of the people in order to give a plentiful supply of bread to the peoplo." The vote was heartily passed and the meeting concluded.

div.head: WIRRAL AND BIRKENHEAD Stiowr
div.p: WIRRAL AND BIRKENHEAD Stiowr

This old-established fixture opens on Tuesday next, and continues over Wednesday and Thursday, and promises to be quite one of the best of the many exhibitions held under the auspices of the Society. The total entry numbers 3,800, which includes exhibits from most of the best known exhibitors through- out the kingdom. On the Wednesday and Thursday evenings, commencing at about seven &clock, a grand naval and military display, also a horse-leapinc, com- petition will take place, in addition to which the Morris Beef Company's team of Clyesdales will again parade, and the Russian Troika will be exhibited. Since the last show was held many alterations and improve- ments have been made at the show yttra, including the providing of two tea gardens, also the enlarging of the tea rooms under the grand stand. The various railway companies have arranged to issue dieap tickets to Liverpool, Birkenhead, or Bebington on each day of the show, so that given fine weather a large number of visitors may be expected, and the result to the Society be the success the Council so richly deserves.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL
The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- ict Council was held on Wednesday afternoon in

Bewsei Chambers. Mr. R. Forshaw presided, and there were present :—Messrs. J. Backhouse, m. Furness, Dr. M urray, A. Brook, W. Mather, J. C. Sutton (clerk), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), H. H. Burnage (assistant surveyor.)

div.head: SE WERING AT PENKETIT.
div.p: SE WERING AT PENKETIT.

_ .• _ The CLERK read a letter from the Pcnketh Parish Council re the Stocks-lane and Station-told sewer. A resolution was passed to the effect that Din, pipes be laid so that it would answer for years to come. Mr. NEWCOMBE thought that a Din, pipe ...would not be sufficient for future developments. Mr. KERFOOT said the sewers could not possibly work with the present Gin. pipe. Dr. MURRAY asked the Surveyor to let him know before the 19th inst. as to the adequacy of a 9-inch pipe and also as to the cost. _ _ _
It was n:oved by Mr. BROOKS, and seconded by Mr. BACKHOUSE, that the matter be refe: red to Dr. Murray with power to act.

COST OF LIGHTING. Mr. FURNESS, referring to the charge maee for gas lamps, said that three or four reductions had been made in the price 'of gas to consumers in the Borough, yet no reduction had Leen made to the Parish Councils. The price of the lamps in Winwick was £2 13s. 4d., in I"'enketh £2 2s. 6d., and Sankey £2 18s. It seemed to him anything but equity that the price should be so much for Sankey. Dr. MURRAY: We are not entitled to any reduction as outsiders? Mr. KERFOOT said that the Corporation said that if a reduction were made the lamps would not pay them. MT. FURNESS said that Sankey Parish Council had been in communication with all the local Parish Councils. They had been trying to arrange a Sub-committee of the various Councils so that they might meet the Warrington Gas Committee. The majority of the Councils were willing to form a committee, but there were some who were not. Mr. MATHER said that it was not the expense of the gas, but the expense of the lighting, the cleaning and the painting of the lamps. Dr. MeRRAY : We pay the lamplighter. Do you Mr. Furness?

Mr. FURNESS : No. Dr. MURRAY : Is it a fact that the lamps do not participate in any reduction? Mr. MATHER : It is a fact. The CHAIRMAN said he thought that the idea of a sub-committee would bring fotth something.

div.head: MOTOR SIGNALS.
div.p: MOTOR SIGNALS.

In the course of Mr. Newcombe's report, the SURVEYOR asked the Council if motor symbols for the purpose of warning motorists could be erected in-stead of boards, close to Sankey school. Mr. FURNESS said be thought it would be all right. Mr. BACKHOUSE : It was awery dangerous position, end something needed to.be done.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSEUM.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSEUM.
Miss Crosfield's Collection of Travel
Souvenirs.

The Museum Committee are indebted to Miss Truck Crosileld for the loan-of the collection of embroidery, metalwork and other objects which she made during her recent tour in the East. The embroideries include several costumes. There are Indian phulcaris, that is, women's robes of red canvas and scarlet silk profusely embroidered, also a robe of purple silk, close set with silken roses, which with a yellow silk bodice embroidered in crimson and vrhite formed a Bakhara girl's festival dress. There are a number of other specimens of Bokbaran embroidery applied to tablecloths, curtains and cushion covers. The characteristic metal work of India is represented by match boxes, rice bowl, a curious lamp in spherical case of perforated brass, and some of the inlaid and coloured brass ware of Moradabad.

The personal ornaments include three quaint brass amulet cases, one encrusted with turquoise, from Til,et, whence comes also a curious old jar of repouss6 copper. Three beautiful necklaces of polished agate, onyx, and lapis lazut€ hail from Kabul. There are several specimens of the pictorial art of India. A num- ber of miniatures on ivory, include portraits of the three great Mogul Emperors and their wives. A small manuscript book exhibits pictorially the story of Rama and Krishna.

Weapons are represented by a wavy Indian dagger,and the sharp-edged iron quoit out of a Sikh turban. Amongst the Syrian objects are a pair of saddlebags showing the inimitable rich colours of the real thing, and a small bowl of enamelled copper in brilliant colours.
The collection, which includes many objects besides those mentioned here, is exhibited in the First Antiqui- ties Room.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
Mr. Sam Livesey's Company in Repertoire.

Mr. Sam Livesey, who is a great favourite with Warrington theatre-goers, has had a fine reception this week, for he • and his powerful company have' pre- sented a most attractive repertoire: On Monday and again last evening" The King of Crime " was played, and the entliusiastid way in which it was greeted shows that this Clever melodrama has lost none of its popularity. Mr. Livesey is seen at his best as Ronjarre, the King of Crime, his realistic portrayal gripping the audience from the very start. He is an actor of great talent and the many exciting ,scenes in which he is concerned held the" house" spell-b ound At the end of each act he was accorded a splendid ovation. Miss Maggie Edwards,as Henriette, Ronjarre's blind wife, acted with power and pa tilos, and Gus Ratcliffe gave a masterly presentment of the unpopular part of Louis Mascorot. There was not. a weak link in the cast and the performance was highly merit9ri- ous in every respect. On Tuesday and Wednesday the play was "Lost by drink" and Mr. Livesey added to his laurels as Coupean, a plumber. On Thursday evening "Called back" was presented with great success, Mr. Livesey again distinguishing himself as Gilbert Vaughan, a blind gentleman, while Miss Maggie Edwards was warmly, applauded for her skil- ful study of Pauline March. To-night "The King of Crime" will again be played.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
Next week Messrs. Skardon and Martin will present their company in the melodrama of circus and sporting life "The way of the world."

div.head: Rev. H. Dunnico and Sunday Observance. Continental Sundays Preferable.
div.p: Rev. H. Dunnico and Sunday Observance. Continental Sundays Preferable.

Preaching in the Kensington Chapel on Sunday even- ing, on" Some Signs of the Times," the Rev. Herbert Dunnico made a sensational attack upon the observance of the English Sabbath. Having referred to the decline in church attendance, be said that, whilst church-going was not everything, the neglect of it was not without significance. For years now railway companies had done their best to encourage Sunday travelling. It was urged that life • was so strenuous that a Sunday of pastime was a necessity for the worker. Did any sane man suggest that the people who patronised Sunday excursions and Sunday picnics were better fitted to resume their duties on Monday morning than those who spent it in a becoming and reverent way ? They knew better. It. was an indisputable fact that crowds who patronised Sunday excursions were more disorderly and rowdy that any others, and protests from all parts of the country conclusively proved this. Moreover, he knew that the crowds who indulged in Sunday sailings were, moreover, much below the usual weekday crowds. More drunkenness, gambling, and general debauchery were seen on board (lifting Sunday than on any other day. They heard a great deal of talk about the Continental Sabbath, but, for his part, he was inclined to prefer it to the English. The early part of the Continental service was always devoted to strict religious observance. In Roman Catholic countries service began about six o'clock in the morn- ing, and went on continuously till noon. It was only after the noon hour had passed that pastimes find recrea- tions were common among the people. If the people of Liverpool would observe their Sabbath from six in the morning till noon they might be excused if they did devote the rest of the day to recreation and rest. In his (the preacher's) opinion we were far more irreligious in this matter of Sabbath observance than the people we were constantly affecting to despise and condemn.
